lessons.title: A Beginner’s Guide
lessons.description: Overview of how the app works and how to start investing with signals.
lessons.body:
Welcome 👋

This app helps you find stock opportunities using data, signals, and market patterns.

Here’s how to get started:

1) Explore Signals
Browse short-term and long-term ideas generated from earnings, momentum, and events.

2) Understand Before You Buy
Open any topic to see the logic behind the signal — not just the result.

3) Start Simple
Focus on a few high-quality ideas instead of overtrading.

4) Track Your Progress
Use the academy to build your knowledge step by step.

The goal is not just to follow signals: it’s to understand them and improve your decisions over time.

Start here 👇

1) Pick 1 stock from Signals
2) Read its Prediction section
3) Buy it virtually
4) Track it for a few weeks

🎯 Goal: understand how ONE trade works

Don’t try to learn everything at once.

Take action first: learning comes after.

lessons.title: Starter Tips
lessons.description: Key investing rules to avoid common beginner mistakes.
lessons.body:
1. Signals

Mixed Signals are AI Signals reviewed by our investment team.

Long Term signals are hand picked signals to buy and hold.

Short Term Signals are automatically generated and adapted to Short Term Trading / Stock Options.

Most AI generated Signals come with both a Short Term AND Long Term view.

AI Signals that underperform over the Short Term tend to rally by the Target Sell Date.

2. Risk Management

Minimize your risks by diversification your exposures: do not put all your eggs in the same basket.

Remember: Past performance is not indicative of future performance.

Investing is risky: never invest money you cannot afford to lose.

Restrain from buying a stock or crypto too big and too fast, especially if you would not hold for the next year in events of short term market downturns.

Save your energy, we are here to help you.

lessons.description: Understand short, mid, and long-term AI price forecasts.
lessons.body:
Price predictions are based on patterns from data, not certainty.

You will typically see:

• Short-term forecasts → driven by unusual trading volume and events

• Mid-term forecasts → influenced by earnings and sentiment

• Long-term forecasts → based on fundamentals and growth

• Very long-term forecasts → driven by industry growth and durable competitive advantages (MOAT)

Use predictions as guidance, not guarantees. Combine them with risk management.

lessons.title: Brokers to Trade With
lessons.description: Recommended brokers and how to choose the right one.
lessons.body:
If you’re just starting out, try to limit yourself to one contract per trade, and no more than one or two plays per week. The goal is to ease into the process and build a feel for how things work without overwhelming yourself.

Starting with a paper trading account can help you practice, but it’s not always realistic — winning can make you overconfident, and losing might discourage you unnecessarily.

Small real-money trades are sometimes more valuable. If you lose, it’s manageable and motivates you to learn; if you win, try to stay grounded, reinvest your net profits into stocks.

The "Ideal Approach" is to start with two types of brokers:
        
1.	A Commission-Free Broker

Platforms like Trade Republic, RobinHood, Saxo, IG, or Interactive Brokers offer "zero-commission trades". 

They may use market orders that include hidden fees or less favorable execution, but they’re ideal for beginners or those investing smaller amounts.

2.	A Premium, Full-Service Broker

Brokers like Charles Schwab or Fidelity prioritize high-quality order execution and offer a wider range of financial products, research tools, and customer service. 

They’re more suitable as your portfolio grows and transaction size increases.


Why Use More Than One?

As your portfolio grows, using multiple brokers provides:

•	Diversification across platforms

•	Reduced settlement risk

•	Access to different features and product ranges

Think of it like portfolio diversification, don’t put all your eggs in one single basket.

Share your country of residence, other members can share their real experiences and recommendations.

lessons.title: Building Your First $5,000 Portfolio
lessons.description: Simple diversification strategy for smaller portfolios.
lessons.body:
A simple way to structure a small portfolio:

• 50–60% in strong, stable companies
• 20–30% in growth opportunities
• 10–20% in higher-risk or short-term ideas

To build a starter portfolio with $5,000 / $10,000, we suggest a bullish approach towards tech stocks, and smart diversification across industries, size, and ownserhip.

1) Allocate 30% of your investment to Long-Term Buy-and-Hold signals:

Apple, Nvidia, and Meta, which together represent 20% of the S&P 500.

2) Allocate 50% of your investment to Mid-Term signals

- Diversify Signals across Industries:
(How the Stock makes money)
Some Tech (e.g. AI Picks),
Some Healthcare (e.g. Eli Lilly),
Some Financials (e.g. Robinhood),
Some Energy (e.g. Nuclear Energy NNE),
Some Consumer (e.g. Lululemon).

- Diversify Ownership:
(Who owns the Stock)
Some Retail Stocks (e.g. Palantir),
Some Institution Stocks (e.g. Apple),
Some Insiders Stocks (e.g. Walmart).

3) Allocate 10% of your investment to Small Caps:
Long Term AI signals (the "Signals" tab), Volatile Industries with great long term prospects:
- Some Quantum Computing (e.g. RGTI, DWave),
- Some Nuclear Energy (e.g. NNE, OKLO),

These names should be either DCA with a long term mindset or played ahead of events (hype)... or both.

4) Allocate 10% for Short-Term strategies:

Pro Traders can allocate 5 to 10% of their portfolio to Stock Options and Crypto.

lessons.title: Strategy Investment Horizon
lessons.description: Choosing the right strategy based on short, mid, or long-term horizon.
lessons.body:
Every investment has a time horizon.

• Short-term → days to weeks (unusual volume, momentum, earnings plays)

• Mid-term → weeks to months (trend continuation)

• Long-term → months to years (fundamentals and growth)

• Very Long-term → couple of years (industry prospects and competitive advantage)

The key is alignment:
Don’t use a short-term strategy for a long-term goal, and vice versa.

Choosing the right horizon improves both timing and risk control.

lessons.title: Sectors Investment Styles
lessons.description: Understand how different sectors behave across market cycles.
lessons.body:
Understanding how each sector aligns with your investment style is key to building a strategy that fits your goals and risk tolerance.

1) Value Investing: Stability Over Speed

Value stocks offer stability and steady growth.

They don’t spike or crash often — instead, they grow gradually, built on strong fundamentals and consistent earnings.

They’re ideal if you want to avoid volatility, but they may underperform growth stocks over the long term.

Sectors:
•	Consumer Staples
•	Utilities
•	Real Estate
•	Industrials

These are large cap value stocks known for stability, strong cash flow, and consistent stable dividends:


•	Coca-Cola (KO) – Iconic consumer brand, steady earnings, strong dividend history
•	Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) – Healthcare giant with reliable profits
•	Procter & Gamble (PG) – Household essentials, defensive during downturns
•	Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B) – Warren Buffett’s holding company, deeply value-driven
•	PepsiCo (PEP) – Similar to KO, strong brand and dividend payer


2) Growth Investing: Volatile but Explosive and Powerful

Growth stocks can drop sharply over the short run, but they also climb much higher over time.

If you avoid panic-selling during dips and choose your stocks wisely with our guidance, you’ll outperform value in the long run.

It’s about handling the volatility and staying in the game.

Sectors:
•	Technology
•	Biotech
•	Fintech

These are large cap companies with strong potential to increase revenue and earnings quickly, often reinvesting profits instead of paying dividends.


•	Nvidia (NVDA) – Explosive growth in AI and chips
•	Meta Platforms (META) – Social and AI innovation, long-term vision in the metaverse
•	Tesla (TSLA) – High innovation and volatility, but massive long-term return
•	Apple (AAPL) – Tech-driven growth with a massive product ecosystem

lessons.title: Boosting a $10k+ Portfolio with Options
lessons.description: How larger portfolios can use options for leverage and yield.
lessons.body:
1. Better risk-reward profile

Options can complement a long-term portfolio, whether it holds $10k+ or a much smaller amount. The aim is to add a carefully sized opportunity for extra returns while keeping most capital in your core investments. Options do not automatically improve a portfolio’s risk-reward profile: the entry price, probability of success and total premium at risk matter.

The app’s strong-buy ideas, AI earnings predictions, buy-the-dip signals and momentum signals can help you research a potential setup. Review the option’s expiration, strike, liquidity and implied volatility as well. A low premium or low implied volatility alone does not make a call a bargain.

Smaller portfolios can sometimes use contracts costing $10 to $40 in total, before fees. For a standard US equity option covering 100 shares, a quoted premium of $0.10 to $0.40 usually means $10 to $40 per contract. These are lower-cost contracts, not necessarily contracts covering fewer shares. Availability depends on the stock, strike and expiry; do not force a trade just to find a cheap option.

2. Limited premium at risk, asymmetric upside

Buying an option outright can provide exposure with a relatively small upfront payment. The purchased option can lose its entire premium, but a favorable move can produce a large percentage gain. That asymmetry is the attraction; it is not a promise of positive returns.

For example, in a hypothetical $2,000 portfolio, a $20 contract represents 1% of capital. If you sell it for $60, the $40 profit adds 2% to the original portfolio value, assuming everything else is unchanged and before costs. If it expires worthless, the $20 loss subtracts 1%. This illustrates how a small position can contribute extra returns, rather than dependable income or guaranteed excess yield.

A $40 contract would put 2% of that same portfolio at risk; in a $500 portfolio it would be 8%. Always judge size relative to your own capital. Cheap contracts can be near expiry or far out of the money, with a substantial chance of expiring worthless.

3. Target the average, not the variance

Options trading is a probability game, just like poker. The goal is not to win every trade, but to make decisions whose potential rewards justify their risks over time. Patience alone does not create an edge, and a few large winners do not prove a strategy will remain profitable.

Look at the combined result after losses, fees and bid-ask spreads. In the example above, one $40 profit offsets two $20 losses before costs. Repeated small purchases can still add up to a large loss, so set a total options budget rather than treating every cheap contract as insignificant.

Use options in small size to support your core portfolio, not to replace it. A correct view on the stock can still lose money if the move arrives too late or implied volatility falls.

4. Stock and Options Risk Rebalancing

If you hold $10,000 in a stock and want to change your exposure, consider the combined risk of the shares and options rather than adding leverage without a plan.

For illustration, moving $1,000 into purchased options leaves $9,000 in shares. If the options double to $2,000 while the shares stay unchanged, the combined position rises to $11,000: a 10% gain, not 20%. If the options expire worthless and the shares stay unchanged, the combined loss is 10%. This is an illustration, not a suggested allocation.

The remaining shares are not protected by buying calls: they can fall too. The premium limits the loss on the purchased option itself before exercise, not on the entire stock-and-options position. The same arithmetic applies to smaller portfolios using smaller dollar amounts.

5. Cash-funded purchases: understand exercise and settlement

You can pay for a purchased option entirely with available cash without borrowing to fund the premium. This discussion concerns buying options outright, not selling uncovered options or other strategies with different loss profiles.

However, standard equity options are generally physically settled, not cash-settled. Exercising a call can require enough money to buy the underlying shares, and in-the-money options may be exercised automatically at expiry. Understand your broker’s rules and manage the position before expiration if you do not want that stock exposure.

For detailed information on options trading, please have a look at the "Options" section.

lessons.title: Intro to Financial Analysis
lessons.description: Key financial metrics every investor should understand.
lessons.body:
Financial analysis helps you understand the strength of a company.

Key things to look at:

• Revenue growth → is the business expanding?
• Earnings (EPS) → is it becoming more profitable?
• Valuation (P/E) → is the price reasonable?
• Debt → is the company financially stable?

Strong companies usually combine growth, profitability, and reasonable valuation.

Use these metrics together: never rely on just one.

lessons.title: Buy the Stock? Is there a Better Alternative?
lessons.description: A checklist to quickly evaluate if a stock is worth buying.
lessons.body:
Before buying a stock, always compare it to similar companies.

Ask yourself:

• Is there a competitor growing faster?
• Is another company cheaper with similar performance?
• Is this the best opportunity in the sector?

Sometimes the best trade is not the obvious one.

Comparing alternatives helps you find stronger risk/reward setups.

Some indicators to consider:

1) Short term trading volume and technical indicators:

•	MACD and Momentum,
•	Support and Resistance levels to watch,
•	Key Fibonacci Levels,
•	Unusual Option activity and Insider trades.

2) Long term Financial Analysis: Financial Growth, Ownership and Social Metrics

•	Revenue Growth and EPS Growth: are they trending up?
•	Short Interest: high short interest could indicate market skepticism.
•	Ownership Data: look at institutional vs. retail ownership.
•	Social Hype Metric: gauge public sentiment and momentum.

3) Analyze Peers, Competitors, and Alternatives by:

•	Market Cap (size and performance).
•	EPS Growth.
•	PE Ratio (for profitable companies).

4) Industry Prospects both for Short Term Volume and Interest and Long Term Demand and Revenues:

• What’s the outlook for the industry? Are there trends or market shifts that could boost demand for the company’s products or services?
• Does the company have a competitive edge in a growing market?

5) For options plays, understand implied volatility and breakeven % upside.

Know how much the stock needs to move for your option to be profitable. Make sure the strike and maturity you chose align with your risk exposures. These are all explained in the Q&A.

6) Review in-app short-term earnings predictions, and long-term financial growth projections.

Understand how the predictions align with the technical and fundamental data.

lessons.title: Look at Momentum
lessons.description: Identify stocks gaining strong buying momentum.
lessons.body:
Momentum describes the strength and direction of a stock’s recent price movement. A stock making higher highs and higher lows may be attracting sustained buying interest, especially if it is outperforming its sector and the broader market. The idea is to identify a trend that has support behind it, rather than assume that a stock must fall simply because it has already risen.

Momentum can be powerful because investors do not all react to new information at once. Strong earnings, improved guidance or a major business development may cause investors to reassess a company over several days or weeks. Some buy immediately, while others wait for confirmation or build positions gradually. That continuing demand can help a price trend persist, although it never guarantees another rise.

Attention can reinforce the move. A breakout may attract traders, appear on more watchlists and draw interest from investors who previously overlooked the company. Short sellers buying shares to close positions can sometimes add to demand. These forces can accelerate a rally, but they can also fade quickly: price strength alone does not prove that the business has become more valuable.

In the app, start with the Unusual Volume sorting metric in the Search tab and review the Momentum Strategy under Short Term Signals in the Q&A. Compare the volume increase with the direction of the price move and look for the catalyst behind it. Heavy volume during a rise may support the case for buying interest; heavy volume during a decline may reflect selling pressure. Unusual volume by itself does not tell you who is trading or whether the move will continue.

Then combine the signal with the app’s other information. Review earnings growth, valuation, relevant news, sector performance and technical indicators such as RSI and MACD. A rising stock supported by improving business results has a different setup from one moving mainly on social hype. RSI can remain elevated during a strong trend, so an overbought reading is a reason to examine the setup carefully, not an automatic prediction that the price will fall.

For a hypothetical example, imagine a stock trading at USD 100 that reports stronger earnings and raises its outlook. It rises to USD 108 on unusually high volume, then pulls back to USD 105 before moving higher again. Holding above its earlier trading range may suggest that buyers are still interested. If the stock instead drops back below that range as selling increases, the breakout may have failed. Neither pattern guarantees the next move; the example shows how price, volume and the catalyst can be assessed together.

The entry price still matters. Buying after a sharp run can leave little room for normal volatility, even when the company’s outlook is improving. Before acting on a signal, decide what would invalidate the trade, how much capital to allocate and how you would manage a reversal. A stop order cannot guarantee its execution price during a gap or fast market. Options add time decay and changes in implied volatility, so a correct view on the stock’s direction can still produce a losing options trade.

Use momentum as one part of a decision, alongside the app’s signals, company analysis and your own time horizon. Watch whether the catalyst remains relevant, whether the stock keeps outperforming and whether the business is meeting expectations. A short-term momentum trade should have a clear review and exit plan; a long-term investment needs a business case that remains convincing even if the momentum disappears. The aim is to participate in strength while recognizing when the evidence has changed.

lessons.title: Look at Beta and Volatility
lessons.description: Assess stock risk and sensitivity to market moves.
lessons.body:
⚡ Risk vs Reward

Before buying a stock, understand how much it normally moves relative to the market.

Beta measures a stock’s sensitivity to market movements:

• Beta 1.0: moves roughly with the market  
• Beta 1.5: may move about 1.5% when the market moves 1%  
• Higher beta: greater potential gains, but also larger declines  

Example: If the S&P 500 rises 2%, a beta-1.5 stock may naturally rise around 3%.

If that stock rises 8% without meaningful company news, the additional move may reflect stronger sentiment, speculation or an overreaction.

This does not guarantee a reversal, but it can indicate that the stock has moved beyond what the market alone would normally explain.

The same works on the downside: if a fundamentally strong stock falls much more than its beta suggests without negative news, it may offer an attractive entry opportunity.

Beta can also help estimate which stocks could rebound more strongly when market sentiment improves.

Compare beta, valuation, growth, recent news and price movements across companies in the same industry.

Among similar businesses, this helps identify which stock offers the best potential upside relative to its risk.

Beta is not a buy signal by itself—it is a reference point for making smarter investment decisions.

lessons.title: EPS (Earnings per Share) Growth
lessons.description: Compare earnings growth to stock price appreciation.
lessons.body:
EPS (Earnings Per Share) growth can indicate a company’s profitability.

Comparing it with price growth helps gauge if the stock’s value aligns with its financial performance or if the stock is over or undervalued.

lessons.title: PE (Price to Earnings) Analysis
lessons.description: Determine if the stock valuation is historically cheap or expensive.
lessons.body:
Examining the historical Price-to-Earnings (PE) ratio shows how the stock’s valuation has fluctuated over time, helping identify if it’s currently trading at a premium or discount compared to its past trends.

Please keep it mind PE ratio does not mean much for stocks that have low EPS. In fact it means nothing for stocks with negative earnings.

It's a good metric for profitable companies with high valuation.

If earnings are negative you want to look at the Revenues growth instead: we like negative earnings stocks if they have steady and high revenues growth.

This is because it could break even and become profitable over the long run.

lessons.title: Compare with Competitors EPS growth
lessons.description: Evaluate company performance versus competitors.
lessons.body: Benchmarking EPS growth against competitors can provide insights into whether a company is outperforming or underperforming its industry peers, offering a clearer picture of its market position.

lessons.title: Compare with Competitors PE
lessons.description: Assess relative valuation across similar companies.
lessons.body:
A cheap stock is not always cheap. Always compare companies within the same industry, since different sectors naturally trade at different valuation levels.

The P/E (Price-to-Earnings) ratio tells you how much investors are willing to pay for $1 of a company’s annual earnings. For example, a P/E of 20 means investors are paying $20 for every $1 of yearly profit.

Typical P/E ranges vary by industry:

* Banks & Insurance: 8–15x
* Energy & Oil: 8–15x
* Consumer Staples: 15–25x
* Healthcare: 15–30x
* Industrials: 15–25x
* Software & AI: 30–60x (sometimes much higher for fast-growing companies)

Because of these differences, never compare the P/E of a software company with a bank or an oil company. Compare businesses with similar business models and growth prospects.

A higher P/E may indicate investors expect faster future growth, while a lower P/E may suggest the stock is undervalued—or that the market expects weaker growth.

Some companies do not have a P/E ratio because they are not yet profitable (they have negative net income). Since you cannot divide by negative or zero earnings to obtain a meaningful valuation, investors often use the P/S (Price-to-Sales) ratio instead.

The P/S ratio compares a company’s market value to its annual revenue. It is particularly useful for young, fast-growing businesses that are investing heavily today and may become profitable later. However, revenue alone is not enough—always compare profit margins as well, since two companies with the same sales can generate very different profits.

Go one step further by comparing the PEG ratio (P/E ÷ Earnings Growth).

The PEG adjusts valuation for expected growth, making comparisons fairer.

A company with a higher P/E can still be attractive if its earnings are growing much faster.

As a general guideline:

* PEG < 1: may indicate undervaluation.
* PEG around 1: often considered fairly valued.
* PEG > 2: may indicate a premium valuation, though exceptional companies can justify higher levels.

Finally, compare revenue growth, EPS growth, profit margins, return on equity (ROE), free cash flow, and debt levels across competitors.

The best investments often combine strong fundamentals, faster growth, and attractive valuations relative to their peers.

lessons.title: Ownership Data Analysis
lessons.description: Understand institutional, insider, and retail ownership.
lessons.body:
Ownership Breakdowns help you assess the risks and volatility of a stock, how much the stock could jump by on earnings date, whether the momentum could go on, whether a panic sell off would affect the stock price.

For optimal portfolio allocations, aim to diversify your exposures across various ownership breakdowns.

By mixing stocks with different institutional and retail ownership ratios, you can balance risk and volatility.

Stocks with higher institutional ownership tend to be more stable, while those with more retail investors might offer higher growth potential but also increased risk.

Diversifying across these categories can help smooth out returns and reduce the overall risk of your portfolio.

1.	Institutional Ownership:
• High (>50%) [MSCI]: Suggests stability and confidence. If increasing, it’s a bullish sign. If decreasing, be cautious.
• Low (<30%): Can indicate a higher-risk stock or an under-followed opportunity.

2.	Retail Ownership:
• High (>40%) [PLTR, SOUN]: Can drive volatility (higher risk and higher reward), especially if based on trends or hype.
• Low (<20%) [MSCI]: May suggest the stock is less popular or undervalued.

3.	Insider Ownership:
• High (>20%/30%) [WMT]: Indicates confidence in the company, lower risks and higher momentum trend. Insider buying is bullish; insider selling may signal caution.

4.	Ownership Changes:
•	Institutional buying or insider buying signals confidence. Selling by these groups could indicate trouble.

Combine this with valuation metrics to get a clearer picture of the stock’s potential.

lessons.title: Short Interest Ratio Analysis
lessons.description: Identify bearish bets or potential short squeezes.
lessons.body:
The short interest ratio shows the percentage of shares being shorted.

A high ratio might signal that investors expect a price drop, while a low ratio often indicates positive investor sentiment.

Short Interest ratio going up is a sell signal.

Short Interest ratio going down is a buy signal.

lessons.title: Social Hype Analysis
lessons.description: Measure investor sentiment and social activity around a stock.
lessons.body:
We track news coverage and look for stocks mentioned most often, alongside discussion on social networks. Repeated mentions can highlight a developing story, upcoming catalyst or growing investor attention.

Check what is driving that attention: earnings, guidance, a product announcement or another event. Read the recent articles and their dates; several stories may repeat the same original news.

More mentions do not necessarily mean positive news, new buying or a higher future price. Compare the coverage with valuation, earnings, price momentum and volume before acting.

Ask which stocks are in the news or why a stock is moving, then open the related research posts to examine the evidence.

lessons.title: Screen Through Alternatives
lessons.description: Compare multiple stocks to find the best opportunity.
lessons.body:
Screening alternative stocks or sectors helps identify better investment opportunities or diversification options.

This step ensures you’re not limiting choices to a single stock or sector.

Select a stock in the Search tab, then tap the compare button, and scroll through metrics to analyse it quick.

You can also compare changes or metrics from the 'Peers' tab for any stock.

These tools are extremely powerful.

lessons.title: Review Predictions and Admin Portfolio Insights
lessons.description: Forecast price moves and professional insights.
lessons.body:
SHORT-TERM predictions focus on upcoming weeks or months.

Stock prices on earnings day are driven by expectations vs reality.

1) Earnings Per Share (EPS)
Measures profitability.
If EPS beats expectations → bullish
If EPS misses → bearish

2) Guidance (Most Important)
Future outlook often matters more than past results.
Strong guidance → price can rise even if EPS is average
Weak guidance → price can drop even after a beat

3) Revenues
Shows business growth and scale.
Important especially for growth companies.

4) Pre-Earnings Positioning
If the stock already moved before earnings, results may already be priced in.

Example:
If a competitor rallies +20% before your stock reports, expectations are already high.

Key idea:
Stocks move based on surprise and pre earnings volume and expectations — not just good or bad results.

lessons.title: pre Earnings CountDown
lessons.description: Tracks stocks approaching earnings dates where volatility and price moves increase.
lessons.body:
A pre-earnings strategy involves taking positions in stocks, options, or other financial instruments in anticipation of a company’s earnings announcement. The goal is to profit from the price movements or volatility changes that typically occur before earnings are released.

This strategy is based on the idea that investor interest and speculative activity often rise ahead of earnings, which can lead to increased demand, higher prices, or elevated implied volatility in options.

How to Profit from Pre-Earnings Based on Interest Rising Ahead of Earnings

1.	Identify Stocks with High Interest Pre-Earnings

•	Look for stocks that typically see a surge in trading volume, search trends, or social media mentions ahead of earnings.

•	Stocks with a history of large earnings surprises often attract more interest.

2.	Use Options to Leverage Volatility

•	Implied Volatility (IV): Before earnings, IV often increases as traders speculate on potential large moves. You can take advantage of this by:

•	Buying Calls or Puts: If you expect a stock to rise or fall sharply based on pre-earnings interest.

•	Selling Options: If you believe the volatility premium is overstated, selling options can capture this inflated value.

3.	Trade the Anticipation, Not the News

•	Price and volatility often rise leading up to earnings but decline after the announcement (known as the “volatility crush”).

•	Enter positions early and exit before earnings are announced to avoid the unpredictable impact of actual results.

4.	Analyze Historical Patterns

•	Study the stock’s historical performance in the days or weeks before earnings.

•	Look for patterns like consistent pre-earnings rallies or volatility spikes.

5.	Leverage Sector and Macro Trends

•	Interest in sectors tied to macro events (like interest rate hikes, tech innovation, or commodity prices) often increases before earnings.

•	Example: If the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, bank stocks may attract pre-earnings interest due to expected higher net interest income.

6.	Monitor Social and Institutional Signals

•	Watch for increased institutional buying, insider activity, or rising mentions on platforms like Twitter or Reddit.

Unusual volume is often the first signal that momentum is building. When trading activity suddenly increases, it usually means large buyers are entering the market and pushing the stock higher.

Momentum then creates a powerful feedback loop:

1) Rising prices attract attention from traders, financial media, and social platforms. Increased visibility brings more buyers and strengthens the move.

2) Strong price performance improves the company’s ability to raise capital at better conditions, strengthening its balance sheet and increasing investor confidence.

3) Price momentum acts as free marketing for the company. More attention can bring new customers, stronger revenues, and further investor demand.

When trading 'unusual volume' stocks, monitor two key indicators:

• Short Interest Ratio – if short interest starts rising significantly, it may signal growing skepticism about the move.

• Earnings Growth – if the stock price keeps rising but earnings do not improve, the momentum may be weakening.

Unusual volume combined with strong momentum can lead to powerful moves, but always watch these indicators to manage risk.

lessons.title: IPO Signals
lessons.description: Monitors newly listed companies and post-IPO trading opportunities.
lessons.body:
IPO Signals: How to Trade and Profit

AI will stock-pick specific IPOs based on company financials and the social hype surrounding their public offering.
          
These signals help identify opportunities for short-term gains or long-term growth.

Why IPOs?

Just like other hype trades, IPOs often generate significant buzz. Early investors benefit from the initial enthusiasm, but timing is critical to avoid losses.

Study Case: Reddit IPO Signal

Reddit went IPO price of $34.
  
Social media FOMO spreads, and within five days, the price jumped to $65, creating a snowball effect, this was a good time to take quick profits.

Those who got in early reaped the rewards, but late buyers risked losses as the price stabilized or dipped.

How to Profit from IPO Signals

IPOs (Initial Public Offerings) can offer significant investment opportunities, but timing and risk management are essential.

Newly listed stocks often experience a cycle of initial excitement, profit-taking, consolidation, and potential long-term growth.

The chart illustrates a typical IPO lifecycle, although actual stock performance can differ significantly.

1. Short-Term Strategy: Trade the IPO Hype

Entry: IPO Day (Week 0)  
Exit: Within the first week

- Buy shares on the IPO date, ideally near the offering price or at an attractive market entry.
- Initial investor excitement, media coverage, and limited share availability can drive strong buying pressure.
- Consider taking partial or full profits during the initial surge rather than chasing higher prices.
- Avoid entering late after a significant rally, when the risk of a sharp correction increases.

Objective: Capture short-term momentum before the initial excitement fades.

2. Long-Term Strategy: Accumulate After the Hype

Entry: IPO Day and/or Weeks 3–4  
Holding Period: 1 year or longer

- Consider opening a small initial position on IPO day.
- Reserve additional capital to dollar-cost average around Weeks 3–4, particularly if the stock pulls back or begins stabilizing.
- The chart illustrates a potential decline extending through Weeks 10–20, meaning investors should avoid committing all their capital too early.
- Continue accumulating gradually if the company's fundamentals, valuation, and growth outlook remain attractive.
- Hold for at least one year when supported by the investment thesis, rather than relying exclusively on short-term price movements.

Objective: Build a long-term position while reducing the risk of buying at peak IPO excitement.

3. Hybrid Strategy: Combine Momentum and Long-Term Investing

Entry: IPO Day  
Profit-Taking: Week 1  
Reentry: Weeks 3–4 and potentially later

- Buy an initial position on IPO day.
- Take partial or full profits during the first week if the stock experiences a strong rally.
- Consider reentering around Weeks 3–4 if prices decline and valuations become more attractive.
- Maintain additional buying power in case the correction continues.
- Hold the long-term position through consolidation and a potential breakout.

Objective: Benefit from early IPO momentum while preserving capital for a more attractive long-term entry.

4. Understanding the IPO Lifecycle

The chart highlights five potential stages:

- Pre-IPO: Private-market speculation increases, but access is generally limited.
- Weeks 0–5 — Hype & Pop: Initial excitement can drive a sharp price increase, followed by profit-taking.
- Weeks 5–20 — Decline: Early momentum may fade as valuations normalize and additional selling pressure emerges.
- Weeks 20–24 — Consolidation: The stock may establish a price floor as buyers and sellers reach a temporary equilibrium.
- Weeks 24–36 — Breakout: Strong fundamentals, earnings growth, and renewed institutional demand may support another rally.

These periods are illustrative, not guaranteed trading windows. Some IPOs rally continuously, while others never recover their initial valuations.

5. Important Catalyst: Insider Selling and IPO Lock-Up Expiration

One of the most important events to monitor after an IPO is the expiration of the insider lock-up period.

What is an IPO lock-up?

A lock-up is a contractual restriction that typically prevents certain company insiders, founders, executives, employees, and early investors from selling their shares immediately after the IPO.

When does insider selling become possible?

- Many traditional IPOs have lock-up periods lasting approximately 90–180 days.
- A common expiration occurs around 180 days, or roughly six months after listing.
- Some IPOs allow earlier partial releases, staggered unlocks, or special exceptions.
- Once restrictions expire, eligible shareholders may sell shares, subject to applicable securities laws, trading windows, and other restrictions.

Why does this matter for investors?

- Lock-up expiration can increase the number of shares available for trading.
- Early investors may realize substantial profits, creating additional selling pressure.
- Anticipation of insider selling can weigh on prices before the actual expiration.
- However, an unlock does not mean insiders will necessarily sell, and the stock may already reflect the expected supply.

Investment strategy: Monitor the exact lock-up expiration dates, the number of shares becoming eligible for sale, and insider transactions before increasing your position.

The six-month lock-up window can overlap with the consolidation and recovery stages illustrated in the chart, potentially creating opportunities for patient investors.

6. Key IPO Investment Insights

- First Week: Strong momentum may create opportunities for short-term profit-taking.
- Weeks 3–4: Initial corrections can offer more attractive entry points.
- Months 2–5: Continued selling or disappointing earnings may create additional accumulation opportunities.
- Months 3–6: Lock-up expirations can introduce new selling pressure and volatility.
- Months 6–9: Stocks with strong earnings, sustainable growth, and attractive valuations may begin a more durable recovery.
- Year 1 and Beyond: Long-term returns increasingly depend on business performance rather than IPO excitement.

7. Potential Tax Benefits

In the United States, holding investments for more than one year generally qualifies gains for long-term capital gains tax treatment, which may be more favorable than short-term rates.

Tax treatment varies by country, tax residency, and individual circumstances.

Final Investment Guidance

Successful IPO investing is not simply about buying on the first day. It requires understanding market psychology, valuation, insider selling restrictions, and the company's long-term fundamentals.

Use AI IPO Signals to identify potential entry points, profit-taking opportunities, and important upcoming catalysts.

Our preferred approach: Avoid chasing excessive IPO hype, take profits when appropriate, maintain capital for potential corrections, and gradually accumulate high-quality companies when valuations become attractive.

Remember: The IPO lifecycle chart represents an illustrative scenario, not a guaranteed price pattern. Always manage position sizes and understand the risks before investing.

8. Options Strategy: Trading IPO Volatility

Options typically become available a few trading days after an IPO, although the exact timing depends on exchange requirements and eligibility.

The first few weeks can create interesting opportunities for options traders, particularly as initial excitement fades and volatility increases.

What to Watch:

- Put Demand: Newly listed IPOs can experience unusually strong demand for puts. This may reflect institutional hedging, bearish speculation, or investors protecting existing positions.
- Insider Hedging: Some early investors may seek downside protection before their shares become eligible for sale. However, lock-up agreements often restrict hedging transactions, so put demand should not automatically be attributed to insiders.
- Implied Volatility (IV): IPO options can carry elevated premiums due to uncertainty. Compare IV with expected price movements before entering a trade.
- Bid-Ask Spreads: Liquidity can be limited initially, particularly for deep out-of-the-money options. Favor liquid strikes and use limit orders to control execution costs.

Potential Options Strategies:

- Buying Puts: Following the initial IPO rally, puts may offer opportunities to benefit from a correction. However, elevated IV and time decay can reduce profitability even when the stock declines.
- Replacing Stocks with Calls: Investors holding IPO shares can sell part or all of their position and purchase call options instead. This reduces capital exposure while maintaining upside potential. The maximum loss on a purchased call is the premium paid, although the option can expire worthless.
- Buying Straddles: Purchasing both a call and a put at the same strike can benefit from a substantial move in either direction. This works best when the realized price movement exceeds the cost of the combined premiums.
- Protective Puts: Long-term investors can purchase puts to establish a downside protection level while retaining their shares. The protection comes at the cost of the option premium.

Timing Considerations:

- Days 1–5 After Options Launch: Monitor put/call activity, implied volatility, and liquidity as the options market establishes pricing.
- Weeks 2–5 After IPO: Initial excitement may fade, creating opportunities for bearish positioning or volatility strategies.
- Months 3–6: Insider lock-up expirations and earnings announcements can introduce additional volatility and potential trading catalysts.
- Months 6–9: As the stock matures, options may offer opportunities to position around consolidation, earnings growth, or a potential breakout.

Our Approach:

We generally prefer taking partial profits during strong IPO rallies and maintaining flexibility as the initial excitement fades.

For investors who want continued upside exposure without committing substantial capital, replacing shares with call options can be an alternative, provided the premium and expiration are attractive.

For bearish setups, we monitor put demand, valuation, technical levels, and implied volatility before considering downside positions.

We also evaluate straddles when we expect substantial price movement but have limited conviction about direction.

Remember: IPO options are highly speculative. A correct directional forecast does not guarantee a profitable options trade. Time decay, implied volatility changes, and execution costs can significantly affect returns.

Use IPO Signals alongside options analysis, position sizing, and risk management rather than assuming that every IPO will follow the same price cycle.

lessons.title: Value at Risk (VaR)
lessons.description: Estimate potential downside risk for positions.
lessons.body:
Value at Risk (VaR) estimates how much a stock could lose over a given time period at a specific confidence level based on historical price movements.

For example, if the 10% VaR is -15%, it means that historically there has been about a 90% chance that losses remained below 15% over the selected time period, and about a 10% chance that losses exceeded 15%. Similarly, if the 1% VaR is -25%, only about 1% of historical periods experienced losses greater than 25%.

One of the main uses of VaR is estimating downside risk before entering a position. Investors can compare the potential downside with their expected upside to determine whether the risk/reward profile is attractive and whether the position size should be adjusted.

When a stock experiences a move close to or beyond its historical 5% or 1% VaR, it often indicates an unusually large sell-off. In some cases, this reflects panic selling or a market overreaction to news. After these extreme moves, market makers, institutional investors, and retail investors may begin buying the dip, increasing the probability of a short-term rebound over the following days or weeks. However, this does not necessarily mean the stock has reached a long-term bottom, as the underlying fundamentals may continue to weaken.

VaR is best used as a statistical indicator rather than a rule. It tends to work better when averaged across many investments and over long periods of time rather than expecting every individual stock to behave the same way. Always combine VaR with financial analysis, valuation metrics, earnings expectations, technical analysis, and your own due diligence before making an investment decision.

You can review the Value at Risk for every stock in the app by opening the stock page, selecting the ||Predictions|| tab in the top-right corner, then viewing the ||Metrics|| section.

- Evaluate how the signal fits into your current industry allocation to ensure diversification across sectors like retail, defense, or others. Refer to the "How to Build a Starter Portfolio" section for guidance.
          
          
2. Company Future Performance and Prediction:

- App Tools: Use the "When to Buy" and "When to Sell" features in the Q&A section, along with financial and technical analysis tools, to make informed decisions.
          
          
3. Position Size and Performance:
          
- If your holding is significant and you want to lock in profits, consider gradually selling to lock in gains (cost averaging out).
          
- If your holding is small and the stock is rising, you might increase exposure by cost averaging a buy if you wish to increase your exposure.
          
- Conversely, if the stock trends downward:
Large Holding with Short Target Sell Date: Cost average a sell out to reduce risk.
Small Holding with Long Target Sell Date: Consider buying more to take advantage of a potential rebound.
          
          
4. Personal Risk Tolerance and Strategy:
          
- Every decision should align with your risk tolerance and overall investment strategy.
- Ensure the signal complements your portfolio allocation and goals.
          
Final Tip:
Balance is key—diversify, cost averaging, use tools available in the app, and stay updated with discussions and predictions for smarter trading.

lessons.title: PE Ratio Analysis
lessons.description: Analyzes valuation using P/E ratios to identify overvalued or undervalued stocks.
lessons.body:
Combine P/E metrics with technical indicators to identify potential value picks and better entry points. The aim is to find companies whose share prices may have fallen further than their business prospects justify. When valuation, earnings growth, and price support align, the setup can offer an opportunity to research a substantial rebound—including potential moves of 50% or more. That is an upside scenario to investigate, not a return the setup can predict with guarantee.

1) Understand both trailing and forward P/E. 

Trailing P/E divides the share price by earnings per share over the previous 12 months; forward P/E uses forecast earnings.

3) Compare PE across peers.

Start with the earnings calendar. In the screener, select Stocks → Earnings Calendar and display Market Cap. Choose a large company reporting within the next two weeks, then tap Competition and sort by P/E. Focus on competitors with similar business models, growth, profitability, and financial strength. Market cap measures company size, while P/E helps assess the price being paid for earnings. Two companies with similar P/E ratios are not necessarily equally attractive.

Compare valuation with the stock’s own history. Use the two-year view to examine changes in share price alongside changes in P/E, then repeat the comparison with a relevant competitor. A rising price with a falling P/E can indicate that earnings are growing faster than the share price. A falling price with a rising P/E can indicate that earnings are deteriorating even faster. This relative-value analysis helps distinguish a potential opportunity from a stock that merely looks cheaper after a decline.

3) Great ideas combine valuation with technical setups. 

A particularly interesting setup is a growth stock trading below its usual P/E range while approaching an established price-support area, provided its earnings outlook remains healthy.

Repeated support tests, improving volume, and a recovery above a recent trading range can strengthen the case for a potential rebound.

Support is an area to monitor, not a guaranteed floor: define what would invalidate the idea before entering.

4) Monitor short interest and short covering.

Track short interest—the shares sold short that remain open—alongside short interest as a percentage of the float and days to cover. Compare these metrics over time to see whether bearish positioning is increasing or easing.

When short sellers close their positions, they buy shares back, which can help support a rebound. Falling short interest alongside a stock holding support or breaking above resistance can strengthen the case for an entry, especially when valuation is attractive and earnings expectations are improving.

Look for confirmation through stronger buying volume and sustained price strength. Short covering alone does not establish a lasting recovery, and reported short-interest data is delayed. Daily short-sale volume is not the same as outstanding short interest.

By August 3, it closed at $307.53, approximately +118.1% over three months. Around the entry, April’s trading highs suggest a resistance zone near $150–$157.

lessons.id: How to set a Stop Loss
lessons.title: How to set a Stop Loss
lessons.description: Automated protection against large losses.
lessons.body:
1. Support Levels

Resistance often occurs around round numbers like $100 due to human psychology.

If the stock breaks through this resistance, it can trigger a sharp decline as fear sets in and people rush to sell, leading to high trading volume and market makers (banks and hedge funds) not supporting the price.

In this cases, setting a stop loss around $95 can help avoid panic sell-offs.

2. Percentage-Based Stop Losses

For options, setting a stop loss based purely on a percentage can be misleading.

Options can fluctuate greatly, sometimes moving from -50% to +100% with relatively small price changes (like -5% to -7%).

In these cases, a fixed percentage stop loss might not be the best approach.

Set a percentage stop loss based on the volatility of the asset!

3. Volatility-Based Stop Loss

Consider the stock’s volatility over the past week when setting your stop loss.

This gives you a better sense of the stock’s typical price swings and helps avoid setting an unrealistic stop loss.

For example, the SP500 volatility is represented by the VIX.

Your stock’s volatility can be calculated by multiplying the stock’s BETA (available in the "Search" tab, scroll to the "Beta" metric) by the current VIX value.

Stock Beta x VIX ~ your stock Volatility

You could set your stop loss to 2x this calculated value for a more tailored approach.

Keep in mind VIX at 15 means 15% volatility, so it would be 0.15 x Stock Beta from the Search tab x Current Stock Price.

4. Fixed Dollar Amount

Decide how much you’re willing to lose in dollar terms and set your stop loss accordingly. This method allows for more controlled risk management.

Note on Stop Losses:

While stop losses can be useful, we’re not huge fans of them, as they may prevent you from benefiting from potential rebounds when you “buy the dip.”

If your broker offers partial stop loss selling, this can be a good alternative, as it allows for cost averaging and gives you more flexibility in managing your position.

Market: What is the VIX?

The VIX (Volatility Index), known as the “Fear Gauge,” measures expected 30-day volatility in the S&P 500. It reflects investor sentiment and market uncertainty.

How to Profit from the VIX:

1.	Trading VIX Derivatives: Invest in VIX-related products like VIX calls, VIX ETFs (e.g., VXX) or VIX futures. These tend to rise when market volatility spikes.

2.	Hedging: Use the VIX to protect your portfolio during market declines, as it rises with increased volatility.

Gauging Greed and Fear with the VIX:

• Low VIX (<15): Signals low volatility and complacency, reflecting market greed.

• High VIX (>30): Indicates high volatility and fear, often during market panics.

The VIX helps investors understand market sentiment and adjust strategies based on shifts in fear or greed.

lessons.title: What is a Hedge?
lessons.description: Protecting portfolios from downside risk.
lessons.body:
What Is a Hedge?

A hedge is a financial position you take to protect yourself from potential losses in your main investments — kind of like buying insurance for your portfolio.

Why Use SPY Puts or VIX as a Hedge?

SPY Puts
	•	A put option on SPY (the S&P 500 ETF) goes up in value if the market drops.
	•	So if your portfolio is full of stocks and the market crashes, your SPY put increases, helping offset losses.

VIX Calls or VIX ETFs
	•	The VIX (a.k.a. the “fear index”) spikes when market volatility rises — usually during crashes or major events.
	•	Owning the VIX or VIX-related instruments (like $VIXY or $UVXY) can profit when panic rises, acting as a buffer.

How Is This Like Insurance?
	•	Just like home insurance, you’re paying a small cost regularly.
	•	If your house doesn’t burn down, your insurance expires worthless — but you’re grateful nothing happened.
	•	Same with a hedge — if your SPY put or VIX option goes to zero, that means the market stayed healthy. That’s a win in itself.

Why Keep Hedge Position Small?
	•	Hedges are not meant to make you rich — they’re meant to protect.
	•	A good rule: 1–3% of your portfolio in SPY puts or VIX exposure is usually enough.
	•	Keeping it small:
	•	Limits cost over time
	•	Avoids eating into gains
	•	Ensures you stay exposed to upside while managing downside.

lessons.title: When to DCA Stocks?
lessons.description: When averaging down makes sense.
lessons.body:
Smarter DCA Framework

1.	Don’t Buy Every Dip
  A stock that rallies +100% can easily drop -50%. If you buy every -5% or -10% pullback, you’ll burn cash too early and watch your portfolio collapse with no dry powder left.

2.	Scale With Magnitude
	•	Large caps: consider adding around -15% to -25%.
	•	Small caps: wait for -30% to -60% before averaging in (especially if they ran up fast).

3.	Size Your Adds
  DCA ≠ doubling down. If a stock dips -30%, consider adding up to +50% of your initial position — not matching it 1:1. This keeps portfolio risk balanced.

4.	Timeframe Matters
  Look at how much the stock gained in the last 3 weeks, 3 months, or 12 months. The faster it ran, the more cautious you should be before averaging down.

5.	Is DCA the Best Choice?
	•	Check for New Buy Signals
Sometimes averaging down isn’t the best move — especially if fresh technical or fundamental signals suggest waiting for a stronger entry point.

	•	Stress-Test Your Emotions
Ask yourself: Would I feel bad if the stock dropped another 20%? If the answer is yes, you may be overexposed and should wait or reduce.

	•	Balance Your Portfolio
Instead of doubling down on one volatile name, consider reallocating into other stocks or sectors that can profit in different market conditions. This way, your portfolio isn’t fully dependent on one trade.

6.	Personal Context
  A.	If You’re Small, You Can Start Early
	•	If your initial allocation is tiny (you planned to build over time)…
	•	If your portfolio is small compared to your net worth…
	•	Or if your annual savings easily replenish cash fast…
👉 Then averaging in earlier is fine — dips don’t have to be huge to justify action.
	B.	If You’re Big, Stay Patient
	•	If your position is already overallocated…
	•	If your portfolio is large relative to net worth…
	•	Or if you have low income and little cash buffer…
👉 Then avoid rushing into DCA. Keep stacking cash and look for value buys instead.

Takeaway:

👉DCA Is a Framework, Not a Rule

👉Adapt it to:
	•	The stock’s volatility (big movers require deeper dips before adding).
	•	Your personal context (net worth, income, risk tolerance).

Be patient, size smart, and only buy dips that are meaningful.

DCA is about balance — keeping enough cash to survive deep drops while still capturing long-term upside.

lessons.title: How to Short
lessons.description: Profiting from falling stock prices.
lessons.body:
How to Short?

Shorting means you’re betting on a stock or the broader market going down in value. 

While traditional shorting requires a margin account and carries significant risk, there are safer and simpler alternatives — especially for retail investors.

1) Use Put Options — Not Margin

We do not recommend using margin accounts. Instead, a more manageable way to express a bearish view is by using put options.

A put option increases in value when the underlying stock or index goes down. 

However, puts are risky — you can lose your entire investment (the premium paid), so proceed cautiously by setting your sotp loss from day 1 (cf onboarding section "Options": "How to set a stop loss").

2) Risk Management Rules

•	Set your stop-loss upfront: Only buy puts where the maximum premium equals the most you’re willing to lose.

•	Limit position size: Never risk more than 1% of your total stock portfolio on a single put option.

•	Avoid short-term expiry: If you’re new, avoid options expiring in less than 2 weeks, as time decay is brutal.

3) Want to Short the Market?

If you want a simple stock alternative to short the broader market, consider VXX stock, which tracks VIX (market volatility).

To understand how VIX works, visit the onboarding section titled “Sell Signals” inside the app "What is the VIX?".

VXX tends to spike when markets drop and volatility surges — but be aware that it loses value over time due to how it’s structured, so it’s best for short-term hedging, not long-term investing.

Always do your own research and remember: Capital preservation matters more than timing perfection.

⚙️ How to Dollar Cost Average (DCA) Stocks and Options

Stocks:

3. Keep Perspective (anything can happen)
Your option premium = max loss — stay patient, skip minor dips, and protect capital for deep entries.

lessons.id: Risk Management Tips for New Joiners
lessons.title: Risk Management Tips for New Joiners
lessons.description: Key principles to protect capital.
lessons.body:
Options can boost your returns when managed properly — but they can also wipe out your investment if not handled with discipline.

Start small, observe the market, and build your experience step by step.


👉Before you start trading options, it’s important to understand the fundamental of "Exposure Allocation":

•	Allocate no more than 10% of your total portfolio to options.

•	If the overall market dips, you lose that 10%.

If the market doesn’t recover, that’s your stop loss — you accept the loss and protect the rest of your capital.


👉When your options double (2×):

•	If your 10% grows to 20% during a market rally, take partial profits.

•	Move half (10%) into safer stocks.

•	Rebalance your options back down to 10%, keeping your risk managed.


👉You should not start trading options without:

•	Reviewing the Options Risk Management onboarding (Explains how to diversify and manage cash.)

•	Reviewing the Stop Loss onboarding (explains why setting your stop loss from day 1 is crucial).


👉With options, your maximum loss is the amount you invest.

Unlike leverage, if an option drops close to 0, it can still bounce back — especially if you trade “out of the money” contracts.

For “deep in the money” options with a delta close to 1, setting stop losses may make more sense.


👉Beyond the Basics: Once you are comfortable managing allocations, you can start exploring volatility strategies like:

•	Buying CALLs and PUTs on the same stock (example: Tesla) — a “straddle” strategy to profit from big moves in either direction.

•	Combining assets like NVIDIA (tech growth) and RGLD (gold stability) for breakout opportunities.

•	Buying VIX to bet on volatility surges.

•	Buying LEAPS deep out of the money for x10/x30 upside.


⚡ Note: You lose if the stocks don’t move much - even if it just goes up slightly — options need sharp moves to pay off - options are timing the market!

lessons.title: Option Stop Loss
lessons.description: How to manage downside risk in options trades.
lessons.body:
Options can lose 100% even if the stock goes up +10%.

Why? Because value depends on more than direction: implied volatility, time decay, and breakeven price all matter. 

A green stock doesn’t guarantee a green option.
    
The best strategy is not to sell an option even if it hits -100%.

Instead you should manage how much you invested in the first place (your stop loss).
        
Why?
        
The amount you invest in options (the premium) is by definition your maximum downside (limited loss).

By definition the amount you invest is your stop loss. 

The optimal strategy to limit losses at -50% (if you want this to be your stop loss) is to invest half the amount you planned on investing in options.

So you should never sell an option even if it hits -100%.

Why?

Because if you sell at -50% and the option picks up to +500% you will be left with the the -50% loss you chose to realize. 

But if you invested half the amount the -50% would be your minimum cap and you could still hit +500% before maturity date.
        
When investing in options, always remember that the amount you invest is your premium—which, by definition, is the maximum loss you can take.

So when should you sell? And what is the best alternative to option if you want to trade leverage with a stop loss?

💡 General rule: 

Hold until expiry unless your position is up 100%+, in which case taking partial profits is a smart move.

📉 Risk vs. Reward

•	Your downside is limited to the premium, but your upside is much greater.

•	If you prefer using stop losses or want to sell ahead of maturity, options would not be the right choice - pure leverage would be a better fit for your strategy.

📌 Options vs. Pure Leverage:

•	Options offer bigger potential gains but come with time decay.

•	Pure Leverage provides more control (with stop losses) but lacks downside protection.

🔄 Selling Strategy:

•	Selling options before they hit +50 to +100% gains often means pure leverage would have been a better choice.

•	Options have convex payoffs (not linear like leverage) but your max loss is capped at the premium.

•	Selling losing options is not a winning strategy; a lower initial premium (investment) is the smart choice.

•	Holding until maturity is best: options down -100% can still recover if the stock rebounds, but if you sell them you are out.

•	The optimal strategy to limit losses at 50% is to invest half your intended amount and treat -50% as your stop loss.

•	With x5 leverage, losses can reach -500%, whereas options cap risk at the premium.

•	Options are cash-based with fixed losses; leverage needs a margin account and can exceed your capital.

•	With leverage, a margin call can wipe you out, while options ensure losses stay within your investment.

•	If deep in the money, holding until assignment can reduce risk, but in most cases, staying in is better.

lessons.title: When to Sell Options?
lessons.description: Signs an option trade should be closed.
lessons.body:
Options trading can be highly rewarding but comes with significant risk. Here are some general guidelines to manage your trades effectively:

1.	Risk Tolerance

•	Options are volatile, and losses can escalate quickly. If you feel uncomfortable or can’t bear a 50% loss, it’s often better to sell the option and minimize your risk.

2.	Start Small

•	For most traders, buying the stock instead of options is a safer choice.

•	If you do trade options, allocate no more than 10% of what you’d spend on buying the stock itself. This helps limit potential losses.

3.	Take Profits Early

•	If your option spikes significantly within a few days, consider locking in profits. Options are highly sensitive to market movements, and waiting too long could lead to disappointment.

4.	Cost Averaging

•	If you bought a large position and the price drops, you can cost average by buying more at a lower price, but this strategy requires careful risk management.

5.	Advanced Strategy for Larger Portfolios

Traders with bigger portfolios who frequently trade options may use a two-leg strategy for diversification:

-	Short Maturity (1 Week): A smaller notional trade for quicker potential profits or to hedge short-term moves (if you buy a put).

-	Longer Maturity (1-3 Months): A larger position to allow time for the trade to play out based on longer-term market predictions.

Key Reminder: Options are speculative and not suitable for everyone. 
Always trade within your risk tolerance, and consider how each trade aligns with your portfolio strategy and financial goals.

lessons.title: Option Cash Management
lessons.description: Managing liquidity and capital allocation.
lessons.body:
Small moves can have a big impact on options, but your downside is always limited to the premium you invest - while your upside is much greater. 
        
It’s important to keep that in mind and treat your premium as the maximum loss you can take.

Cash management is key. 

You will receive alerts that keep emphasizing taking profits and holding cash because when a broader market dip happens, if all your options have near-term maturities and you just bought them a week ago, you could be wiped out.

🚨 Diversification is crucial:

✅ Spread out maturities - from 1 month to 1 year

✅ Stagger your option entries — don’t buy all at once - buy slowly over time

✅ Diversify across stocks — buy at least 10 different stocks (this one’s obvious)

🚨 Allocation and rebalancing is crucial:

✅ Never allocate more than 10% of your stock portfolio to options.

✅ If your option allocation grow to 15%, take profits and rebalance the excess 5% back into cash or stocks.

✅ A broad market dip can wipe out options before maturity, but with stocks, you can hold through the downturn and recover.

Take partial profits, hold cash, and be prepared in case of a real crash—if the S&P 500 drops 10%, wait for a 30% to 50% dip in the stock before adding more options (cf when to buy the dip section).

lessons.title: How to Cost Average Options
lessons.description: Strategies to improve entry price.
lessons.body:
To cost average an option, the general approach is to wait for a significant price drop in the underlying stock before buying more options. 
        
Here’s how you can approach it:

1.	Wait for the Stock to Dip:

•	Large Caps: Wait for the stock to dip by 30% from your initial entry price before buying more options.

•	Small Caps: You may want to wait for a 50% dip in the stock’s price before considering more options.

2.	Follow Cash Management Guidelines:

If you have extra cash to invest, make sure you’re managing it wisely to protect your portfolio from excessive risk:

•	Diversify: Don’t put all your money into the same stock; spread it out by buying options in other stocks.

•	Spread Out Maturities: Buy options with different expiration dates to reduce the risk associated with timing.

•	Stagger Your Entries: Avoid buying all options at once. Instead, spread out the purchases over time to mitigate broader market risk.

Cost averaging in options requires patience and disciplined entry points, you won't be able to buy all the dips.

Keep in mind the option price is driven by the stock price, and the amount invested in options (the premium) is by definition your maximum loss (stop loss). 

By following these guidelines, you’ll be able to manage risk while maximizing potential gains.

lessons.title: When to Roll Options?
lessons.description: Extend option positions when needed.
lessons.body:
Rolling an option means closing your current position and opening a new one with a later expiration (and sometimes a different strike).

You might consider rolling if:

1.	You’re still bullish (or bearish) but your thesis needs more time to play out.

2.	Your current option is losing value due to time decay (Theta), but the underlying stock still looks promising (Refer to the ‘When to Cost Average Options’ part of the onboarding for more information).

3.	You want to reduce your risk or improve your breakeven, perhaps by selecting a lower-cost strike further out.

4.	You want to avoid assignment (for short options) or reduce margin requirements.

lessons.id: Why Options Have Lower Win Rate than Stocks
lessons.title: Why Options Have Lower Win Rate than Stocks
lessons.description: Options require larger price moves.
lessons.body:
It’s natural for options to have a lower win rate — that’s because to be profitable, the underlying stock usually needs to move at least +8% or more, just to cover the cost of the option.

But here’s the upside: when options win, they win big.

Some of our AI picks have returned up to x35 (+3,400%) from just a +100% move in the stock. In bull markets, it’s common to see options return x5 to x10.

Like stocks, options come with ups and downs — sometimes you’ll hit a x5, other times it might go -100%. That’s the nature of high-reward strategies.

Stocks tend to have higher win rates but lower gains, while options are the opposite — lower win rates, but massive potential returns.

To succeed with options, review the option onboarding material:

•	Master cash management

•	Set smart stop-losses

•	Learn when to cost-average

•	Follow your allocation and rebalancing plan

Stick to the methodology and stay consistent — over time, the math works in your favor.

lessons.id: Should I sell my 1 Single Option?
lessons.title: Should I sell my 1 Single Option?
lessons.description: Managing small option positions.
lessons.body:
Whether to sell your single option depends on a few key factors, but here are some helpful guidelines:

👉 Most signals are triggered with a bullish view, and momentum often continues after the alert, making it tempting to hold. 

That said, you want to be strategic, not just hopeful.

Ask yourself two key questions:

1. What upcoming events could drive further upside?

Is there an earnings report, product launch, competitor earnings, or a conference that could spark more interest? 

If so, holding might make sense — but only if you’re prepared for volatility.

2. How much of your portfolio is this option?

Options can swing from +100% to -100% very fast.

• If the position now makes up more than 2–3% of a large portfolio (e.g. close to your annual savings or net worth), it may be wise to lock in profits.

• If you’re trading with a small portfolio (e.g. size of 1 month’s savings), letting it run even up to 10% exposure might be fine if you’re comfortable losing it all.


A few strategies to consider:

• Sell at +100% and rotate into the underlying stock (sell the option, buy the stock instead).

• Sell the option and buy a smaller, out-of-the-money option with shorter maturity — this lets you lock in profits while still staying in the game.

• Or sell and rotate into a small position in a leveraged ETF for exposure with less capital at risk.

At the end of the day, diversification is key — it’s often smarter to take profits and reinvest into smaller, diversified opportunities.

You’re never wrong to take profit. Protect your gains and think long-term!

lessons.title: Shorting and Puts
lessons.description: Ways to profit from declining markets.
lessons.body:
Shorting in an Inflationary Market: Use With Caution

In today’s environment, shorting is extremely tactical and high risk.

The market’s long-term inflationary drift makes being short a tough game — especially when trading with margin or short-dated puts.

Risks - Why Shorting Is Tough:

•	Inflation pushes everything up over time — puts often expire worthless unless the stock drops sharply (≥8%).
•	Margin amplifies losses and can force you to exit at the worst moment. Cash-only is safer in this climate.
•	Shorting hype rarely works unless volume, price, and sentiment all shift decisively.

Signals - When Shorting Can Work:
•	Post-hype trades in the Signals Tab, (e.g., after IPO runs or “Pelosi trades”, or other short dated Buy Signals) where the story fades.
•	Famous short seller releases in the Social Feed — use momentum and fear spikes to ride the reaction.
•	Index rebalancing drops release in the Social Feed — when a stock gets kicked from a major index.
•	Macro events — pre-FOMC dips or market-wide fear triggers (but time your exit tightly).

Key Principles:
•	Shorting = precision game.
•	Use defined risk (small position sizing, no margin blow-ups).
•	Avoid overconfidence — long-only often performs better over time.

Bottom line: If you’re going to short, treat it as a tactical move, not a strategy. Most traders are better off focusing on long setups and patiently waiting for broader entries.

For more, search #SHORT in the feed for strategies, setups, and smart comments.

lessons.title: Sensitivities: Delta of a Call
lessons.description: Measure option price sensitivity to stock moves.
lessons.body:
Delta measures how sensitive your option is to the stock’s price — but it also shows the probability it ends up in the money at expiration.

• Delta ≈ 1 → Deep in-the-money call (high chance to finish profitable)
• Delta ≈ 0 → Deep out-of-the-money call (very low chance)
• Delta ≈ 0.5 → At-the-money (about 50/50 odds)

So if your call option has a delta of 0.6, it means two things:

1. For everything else being equal, the option price moves ~$0.60 for every $1 move in the stock.
2. You have about a 60% chance of finishing in the money: the closer you are to maturity, the 'sharper' your delta.

lessons.title: Sensitivities Greeks: Gamma of a Call
lessons.description: How delta changes with stock price.

lessons.title: Sensitivities: Delta and Gamma of a Put
lessons.description: Understanding put option sensitivity.
lessons.body:
Put options also have Delta and Gamma, just like calls.

• Delta tells you how much the put price changes when the stock moves.
• Gamma tells you how quickly that Delta changes.

For puts:
• Delta is negative, because puts usually rise when the stock falls.
• Example: a Delta of -0.40 means the put may gain about $0.40 if the stock drops by $1, all else equal.

Gamma:
• Gamma is usually highest when the option is near the strike price and close to expiration.
• High Gamma means your Delta can change very fast, which makes the position more reactive but also riskier.

Simple way to think about it:
• Delta = sensitivity
• Gamma = acceleration of that sensitivity

If you are new to options, focus first on Delta. Gamma matters most when trading shorter-dated options.

lessons.id: How to 20x with Options: Long Term
lessons.title: How to 20x with Options: Long Term
lessons.description: Long-term option strategies for asymmetric returns.
lessons.body:
How to 20x with Options: Strategy 1, LEAPS.

Goal: Hit massive upside on small caps with long-dated calls

•	Buy long-term maturity call options (9–18 months out), 

•	Strike 50%+ out-of-the-money.

•	Place a limit order at the mid — not a market order — because these are illiquid and spreads are wide.

•	If the stock doubles or triples over time, your option could return 10x–30x.

•	This strategy requires patience — think small-cap tech or biotech with high growth potential.

•	Diversify your LEAPS picks, and follow the position sizing rules outlined in the app onboarding for option risk management.

This strategy requires patience. Diversification, sizing, staggering entries and discipline are critical. 

The app’s onboarding provides exact formulas — stick to them.

lessons.id: How to 20x with Options: Short Term
lessons.title: How to 20x with Options: Short Term
lessons.description: Short-term high-risk, high-reward option strategies.
lessons.body:
How to 20x with Options: Strategy 2, 0DTE (Same-Day Expiry Options).

Goal: Explosive short-term gain — or total loss

•	Buy options expiring the next day (“0DTE”), slightly out of the money (3–5%).

•	These can return 15x–20x overnight if the stock makes a big move on earnings, news, or momentum.

•	But if it doesn’t move enough — your option can go to zero overnight.

•	This is a lottery ticket approach: only use small size, diversify across a few names, and follow strict cash management.

Used well, this strategy can multiply capital fast — but also destroy it just as quickly.

Diversification, sizing, staggering entries and discipline are critical. 

The app’s onboarding provides exact formulas — stick to them.
