lessons.title: What is a Call Option?
lessons.description: A contract giving the right to buy a stock at a fixed price.
lessons.body:
A call option pays out when the stock price exceeds the strike price on Maturity Date.

• Payout: The option pays the difference between the stock price and the strike price, minus the premium paid.

• Example:
• Strike Price = $50
• Stock Price at Expiration = $60
• Payout = ($60 - $50) - Premium Paid

• Payout when stock price > strike price: If the stock price is below the strike price, the call option expires worthless.

• The premium (the cost of the option when you buy it) is the maximum loss.

• Implied volatility (explained in the Option Q&A) is crucial in options pricing. Higher volatility increases premiums, making options more expensive.

• Volatility vs. Stock Movement: If the stock price goes up but volatility drops, the value of a call option might decrease. This is because lower volatility limits the potential for larger price moves, reducing the upside.

• Tip: Sometimes it’s better to wait a few hours after market open when volatility is lower, as this can lead to cheaper premiums and more potential upside for calls.

lessons.title: What is a Put Option?
lessons.description: A contract that profits when the underlying stock falls.
lessons.body:
A put option pays out when the stock price falls below the strike price at expiration.

• Payout: The option pays the difference between the strike price and the stock price, minus the premium paid (which is the cost of the option when you buy it).

• Example:
• Strike Price = $50
• Stock Price at Expiration = $40

• Payout = ($50 - $40) - Premium Paid

• Payout when stock price < strike price: If the stock price is above the strike price, the put option expires worthless.

• The premium (the cost of the option when you buy it) is the maximum loss.

• Implied volatility (explained in the Option Q&A) is crucial in options pricing. Higher volatility increases premiums, making options more expensive.

• Volatility vs. Stock Movement: If the stock price goes up but volatility drops, the value of a call option might decrease. This is because lower volatility limits the potential for larger price moves, reducing the upside.

• Tip: Sometimes it’s better to wait a few hours after market open when volatility is lower, as this can lead to cheaper premiums and more potential upside for calls.

lessons.title: Stocks VS Options?
lessons.description: Understand differences in leverage, risk, and payoff.
lessons.body:
Options rise when stocks rise, but stocks can rise while options fall!
          
Options are juste like crypto: the safest choice is to buy stocks and hold until the target sell date in blue (explained in the onboarding screenshots).'

Why?

Because you might lose money even if the stock goes up by +10%! 

With stocks, if you hold until the target sell date (and resist the urge to panic sell early), your win rate climbs to 80%.

The Target Sell Date is highlighted in blue (explained in the onboarding screenshots).

Remember: Options are not part of the membership, you signed up for Stock Research.

Yet many are focusing on them because they got already got $100,000 to $1 Million in stocks and enjoy using leverage in small % of their portfolio.

This is explained in the Allocation section of the app: How much Options should you buy?

Options are not “safe.” 

Allocate only 10% of your portfolio, just like you would do with crypto - accepting you may lose option trades, with the hope that the winners excessive yields cover the losses and more.

What we accomplished with META, TSLA, ADSK, HOOD, SHOP, AMZN, PLTR, SOUN, RGTI, ORCL, SMCI, MSTR, META, NFLX and others options that went x5 to x35... most people can't achieve this yield in a lifetime.

Stocks - held until the target sell date - safer and will deliver a 70% to 90% win rate.

Options will deliver a lower win rate, but some plays like SOUN delivered x34 (+3300%) within a month, something you cannot expect to achieve with stocks (SoundHound ai stock gained +150%).

If you play options, make sure to split the amount in smaller lots and buy at least 10 to 20 plays: diversification is key, do not put all your eggs in the same basket, and focus on quality over speed and quantity!

lessons.title: Are Options the same as Leverage?
lessons.description: Options provide leverage but behave differently from margin.
lessons.body:
Are Options the same as Leverage?

No, Options and Leverage are not the same.

With Options, your maximum loss is capped at the premium paid. However, the leverage you get depends on several parameters like the strike price, current stock price, and time to maturity.

Refer to the ‘Option Signals’ section in the Q&A to understand how each parameter (Strike, Maturity, and Current Stock Price) affects the leverage in options trading.

lessons.title: Option Signals
lessons.description: How to apply AI signals when trading options.
lessons.body:
Every stock research idea can also be traded using call options. When a stock price rises, call option prices generally rise as well. The difference is that options provide leverage, meaning they can amplify both gains (unlimited asynmetric upside) and losses (limited downside).

Where to find signals:

* "Signals" tab → "Stocks & Options Signals"
* Select "Options Predictions" to view suggested Strike and Maturity.  
* "Signals" tab → "Admin Insights"

How to choose the right option:

Your strike price and maturity should match your investment strategy:

1. Time Horizon

* Short-term view: ~1 month maturity
* Medium-term view: 3–6 months maturity
* Long-term view: 6–12 months (LEAPS)

Longer maturities provide more time for the investment thesis to play out and generally reduce time decay.

2. Position Size (amount invested)

* Higher strike prices: Higher potential returns, but higher short term risk (cf the "Options Predictions" convexity graph in the "Signals tab).
* Lower strike prices (near or in-the-money): Lower risk, higher probability of success, but lower convexity and upside.

Choose your Strike based on how much you’re comfortable risking.

3. Bid & Ask Spread

Always review the option chain before buying. Wide bid/ask spreads can significantly impact your entry price.

Review the Limit Orders, Market Orders, and Bid/Ask sections before placing your first options trade.

Beginner Guidelines

* Use small position sizes while gaining experience.
* Increase exposure gradually as your knowledge and confidence grow.

Remember: Options can generate larger returns than stocks, with tail signals delivering 30X to 100X overnight, but they also carry higher risk. Proper position sizing, patience, and disciplined execution are essential for long-term success.

lessons.id: Option Signals are Also Stock Research
lessons.title: Option Signals are Also Stock Research
lessons.description: Every option signal reflects a stock view: you can trade the stock instead.
lessons.body:
If you see a call-option signal, you can simply buy the stock instead. If you see a put-option signal, you can reduce, sell or avoid the stock.

Example: If we expect Apple to rise and share a call option, stock investors can ignore the strike and expiration and buy Apple shares directly.

The expected stock direction is the same. Options simply add leverage and expiration risk, while shares provide direct ownership and can be held longer.

You never need to trade options to use our signals—choose stocks or options based on your experience and risk tolerance.

1) Stocks and Options: Why We Cover Both

Stocks and options are closely connected because an option’s value is primarily driven by the movement of its underlying stock.

A bullish stock research can support buying the stock, a call option or a longer-term LEAPS call. A bearish signal can support selling the stock, reducing exposure or buying a put option.

This is why stock and options signals can often be used together. The expected direction is usually the same, but the risk, leverage and timing are different.

2) How Stocks Work

Buying a stock gives you direct ownership in a company.

• Stocks do not expire.

• Your profit or loss generally moves in line with the share price.

• You can hold through short-term volatility if the long-term thesis remains valid.

• Stocks are generally more suitable for gradual entries, DCA and larger portfolio allocations.

Example:

A stock trades at $100 and later rises to $120.

If you invested $1,000, your position would gain approximately 20%, becoming worth around $1,200.

3) How Options Work

An option gives you the right—but not the obligation—to buy or sell a stock at a specific strike price before an expiration date.

• Call options generally benefit when the stock rises.

• Put options generally benefit when the stock falls.

• Options provide leverage, allowing a smaller investment to control exposure to more shares.

• Options provide limited loss, allowing a full capital loss to be limited to a smaller investment.

• Options can expire worthless if the expected move does not happen in time.

• Their value is also affected by volatility, strike price and time decay.

Example:

A stock trades at $100, and you buy a call option with a $105 strike.

If the stock quickly rises to $120, the option could gain significantly more than the stock on a percentage basis. However, if the stock remains near $100 until expiration, the option could lose most or all of its value—even if the company remains a good long-term investment.

4) Using Bullish Signals

Imagine you receive a bullish signal on a stock trading at technical support.

A stock investor could:

• Buy a small position immediately

• Add gradually through DCA

• Hold without worrying about expiration

An options trader could:

• Buy a call for a short-term move

• Buy a 6–12 month LEAPS call for a longer-term thesis

• Use a call spread to reduce the upfront cost

The same bullish signal supports each approach, but the appropriate trade depends on risk tolerance and expected timing.

5) Using Bearish Signals

Imagine we expect a stock or the broader market to decline.

A stock investor could:

• Trim the position

• Sell the position

• Keep cash available for a lower entry

An options trader could:

• Buy a put

• Use a put spread

• Hedge an existing stock position with protective puts

Again, the underlying signal is the same—the implementation is different.

6) Why Covering Both Is Important

Stock investors can benefit from options analysis because options activity can reveal expectations around volatility, support, resistance and upcoming catalysts.

Options traders need the stock analysis because the underlying company, chart, valuation and market conditions ultimately drive the trade.

Covering both allows investors to:

• Use stock research for shares, calls, puts or LEAPS

• Select the instrument that best matches their time horizon

• Compare lower-risk ownership with leveraged exposure

• Hedge existing positions during uncertain markets

• Participate without allocating the same amount of capital

• Adjust risk based on portfolio size and experience

7) Choosing Between Stocks and Options

Stocks may be more appropriate when:

• You have a long-term investment thesis

• You want to use DCA

• You are uncertain about the timing of the move

• You prefer lower leverage and no expiration date

Options may be more appropriate when:

• You expect a specific move within a defined period

• You understand strike selection, expiration and time decay

• You want defined risk or leveraged exposure

• You keep the position small enough to lose the entire premium

8) The Key Takeaway

Stock and options signals are connected because both depend on the underlying stock’s movement. However, they are not identical: stocks offer direct ownership, while options add leverage, expiration risk, volatility exposure and time decay.

The market thesis may be the same, but the correct instrument depends on your timing, experience, portfolio size and tolerance for risk.

lessons.title: How Cheap is Your Option?
lessons.description: Evaluate option pricing relative to volatility.
lessons.body:
Wondering if that option is a steal or overpriced? Our app’s got you covered with a powerful feature—Implied Volatility (IV) signal and Breakeven % Upside analysis! 📊



1) Implied volatility tells you how much the market thinks a stock will move.

The higher the IV, the pricier the option, because there’s a bigger chance it’ll end up profitable.

Our app compares the option’s IV between similar stocks and does it with with its historical volatility as well, helping you instantly see if you’re getting a good deal or paying too much.



2) Check out how much the stock needs to rise if held until maturity just to breakeven! 📈 This is determined by analyzing the Strike Price and the Premium (the cost of your option).

Different stocks have different prices, so a $5 option on one stock might be a bargain (if the stock price is high), while on another, it could be a rip-off (if the stock price is low).

Breakeven % Upside = (Strike + Premium) / Current Stock Price



Our app compares the option’s Breakeven % upside between stocks, helping you instantly see if you’re getting a good deal or paying too much.

Take advantage of this great features to make smarter, more informed trades. Go in the "SEARCH" tab and sort the stocks by "Implied Vol" rather than "Valuation"!💡

lessons.title: Options Time Decay
lessons.description: Why options lose value as expiration approaches.
lessons.body:
Options Time Decay (also called theta decay) is the gradual loss of value in an options contract as it gets closer to expiration.

• Why it happens: Options have a time value. The closer you get to expiration, the less time there is for the option to become profitable — so its value drops.

• Who it hurts: Buyers of options (calls or puts) lose value over time if the price doesn’t move in their favor.

• Who it helps: Sellers of options benefit from time decay, as they collect premium and hope the option expires worthless.

Example: A call option worth $5 today might be worth only $2 in a week — even if the stock price doesn’t change — just because time ran out - visuals explained in the video.

lessons.title: Bid and Ask: Best Execution Price
lessons.description: Understand spreads and order execution.
lessons.body:
In trading, the bid is the highest price a buyer is willing to pay, and the ask is the lowest price a seller is willing to accept.

Here’s how it works with an example:

Imagine an Apple’s market price is $1. What’s actually happening is that buyers are bidding at $0.90, and sellers are asking $1.10.

This $1 is just an average reference point, but the trade won’t happen at that price—it will happen at the bid or ask when someone accepts one of these prices.

If you place a limit order at $1 (midpoint), you’re trying to buy at a price between the bid and the ask. But if prices move up, you may not get filled because your offer is lower than what sellers now want. You essentially become the new highest bid.

On the other hand, if you use a market order, you’ll match the current bid or ask instantly. This means you would buy at $1.10 or sell at $0.90, depending on which side of the transaction you’re on.

Market Makers (banks and sometimes hedge funds) profit from the spread between bid and ask. For instance, if they sell an option at $1.10 and then buy it back at $0.90, they make $0.20.

However, they risk loss if prices move unfavorably (e.g., selling to you at $1.10 and then needing to buy it back at $1.20).

This spread helps market makers manage the risks of sudden price movements and ensures liquidity, making it easier for others to buy and sell.

lessons.title: Market Order vs. Limit Order
lessons.description: Choose how you want trades executed.
lessons.body:
1) Market Order: If you want your order to be filled immediately, you can use a market order, which will match the current bid or ask price.

This is fast but doesn’t guarantee a specific price. You might end up buying at a slightly higher ASK or selling at a slightly lower BID than expected.

Market orders are typically chosen for urgent trades, where entering or exiting a position quickly is more important than getting the best price.

2) Limit Order: If you’re patient and want to control your purchase price, you can set a limit order.

For instance, placing your limit order at the MIDpoint between the BID and ASK can save on costs compared to the market order.

However, if prices move in the opposite direction (for example, the price goes up while you’re trying to buy), your order might not be filled, and you could miss the opportunity. This method is preferred by traders who prioritize cost and can tolerate a slower fill time.

lessons.title: How to Copy Trade?
lessons.description: Replicate signals without impacting pricing.
lessons.body:
When an option signal is sent, avoid buying the exact same strike and maturity. 

If we all buy the same strike and maturity it can widen the bid-ask spread.

Instead, wait or choose nearby strikes/maturities.

This way, you avoid poor fills and keep pricing efficient.

Please have a look at the "Bid and Ask" section of the option unboarding to understand what is the price of an option and how the order book works.

lessons.id: Buy to Open vs. Buy to Close
lessons.title: Buy to Open vs. Buy to Close
lessons.description: Understand opening and closing option trades.
lessons.body:
1) Buying a Call: When you buy a call option, you’re betting the stock will go up.

If it does, you profit by the difference between the stock price at maturity and the "strike price" (the agreed-upon price), minus the premium you paid to open the option (cost of the option).

Essentially, someone else has sold you this call, and will owe you if the price rises.

2) Selling a Call: You can also sell a call, where you receive the premium upfront.

However, if the stock price goes up, you will owe the buyer the difference between the strike price and the final stock price at maturity.

Selling options has higher risk, as losses could be unlimited if the stock price rises significantly.

- Buy to Open: When you buy an option for the first time, you're "opening" the position.

- Buy to Close: If you've sold an option first and now want to "close" out that position, you would buy it back. But if you’re only buying options and not selling them to begin with, "buy to close" doesn’t apply—you’d only focus on "buy to open"

For now we mostly 'buy to open' call options!

lessons.title: What is a Call Spread?
lessons.description: Defined-risk bullish options strategy.
lessons.body:
A call spread involves buying a call option and selling another at a higher strike price with the same expiration.

• Lower cost: Selling the higher strike reduces the upfront cost.
• Limited risk & reward: Caps both your potential profit and loss.

Great for when you expect a moderate rise in the stock price, not a big jump.

Example: You buy a call at $50 and sell another at $55. If the stock rises to $55, you profit up to the difference ($5), minus the cost of the spread. If it stays below $50, you only lose the upfront cost.

lessons.title: What is a Straddle?
lessons.description: Strategy that profits from volatility in either direction.
lessons.body:
What is an option Straddle and how to Replicate performance with Stocks?

1) A straddle is an options strategy where you buy a call and a put with the same strike price and expiration. It profits from significant price movement in either direction but loses if the stock price remains stable.

When you buy a straddle, you are buying volatility—you expect the stock to move sharply upward or downward.

Example: You buy both a call and a put at a $100 strike price. If the stock moves significantly—to $110 or $90, for example—one option may generate enough profit to cover the cost of both. If the stock remains close to $100, you may lose the premiums paid.

2) A stock-and-cash alternative can provide partial downside flexibility without using options. Buy half of your intended stock position now and keep the other half in cash. Invest the remaining half after a chosen interval, such as one week or one month.

That second purchase date represents the time horizon over which you expect the strategy to play out. If the stock rises, your first half participates in the gain, and it is a good time to take profits. If it falls, you hold your initial stock position and your reserved cash lets you buy the second half at a lower price.

This is a staggered-entry strategy, not a true straddle: it reduces timing risk but does not directly profit from a falling stock price.

lessons.title: What is a Covered Call?
lessons.description: Generate income from stocks you hold.
lessons.body:
What is a Covered Call?

A covered call is an options strategy where you:
•	Own a stock, and
•	Sell a call option on that stock.

You earn a premium upfront, but agree to sell the stock at a set price if it rises above that level before the option expires.

Example:

You own 100 shares of Apple at $180.

You sell a $190 call option and get $2/share (x100=$200 total for the contract).

•	If Apple stays below $190 → you keep the shares and the $200.
•	If Apple rises above $190 → your shares are sold at $190, and you keep the $200 premium + profit on the stock.

This strategy works best when you expect sideways or modest gains in the stock.

lessons.title: Trading Options on the S&P500
lessons.description: Strategies for trading index volatility.
lessons.body:
ETFs like SPY are often used as proxies for trading S&P 500 options, but they are passive investments not inherently designed for active options trading, because there are many things to take into account (many stocks).

Strategies You Can Try

1.	Selling Ahead of Macro Events

•	Before key economic announcements (e.g., CPI, PCE, or Fed meetings), the market might dip as traders hedge.

Buying puts a week ahead of this period and buying calls the day before the announcement can be profitable if there is no major concern released.

2.	Seasonal Trades

•	August/September: Consider buying puts in late August to anticipate the typical post summer / new start of the year September dip.

•	December: Buying S&P 500 calls before Christmas can capture potential year-end rallies, as people reallocate funds or buy the dips sold off mid December for tax purposes.

3.	Market Calendar Yield

•	Leverage the S&P 500 Market Calendar Yield in the "Short Term" Signals (in the "Signals" tab) to identify statistically favorable trading periods.

Volatility and Risk

•	VIX as a Guide: The VIX index reflects the implied volatility of S&P 500 options. Use it to gauge how much you’re paying for options’ volatility. High VIX often indicates pricier options but also greater potential price swings.

•	Theta Costs: Remember, rolling options (extending their maturity) costs money due to time decay. Rolling options aren’t always good. You pay for theta, when you buy options the timing is crucial.

Example:

Typically #NVDX (NVIDIA options rolled) paid 0% over 2024, yet the stock gained +200% in 2024. Timing is crucial when trading options.

Challenges with Options

Options trading is complex and often unprofitable for most traders. Success requires exceptional timing and a disciplined approach: It’s very hard to be profitable with options. If you are, you’re doing great at timing the market!

Personal Preference

Overall, most people better invest in stocks instead. This simplifies the approach and avoids the pitfalls of options’ complexities.

lessons.title: MacroEconomic Events
lessons.description: Key macro releases that can move markets.
lessons.body:
Macroeconomic events provide key insights into inflation, employment, and monetary policy:
        
- CPI (Consumer Price Index), 
- PPI (Producer Price Index), 
- NFP (Nonfarm Payrolls), 
- and FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee).
        
These events can move markets and impact short-term trends.

How traders typically play these events?

• Major macroeconomic releases often create a predictable pattern in markets.
• Ahead of the event, traders frequently reduce risk and hedge positions, which can lead to fear-driven selling the day before or early the same day. 
• This is why puts or defensive trades sometimes work well leading into major releases like CPI or Fed decisions.
• Once the data is released, the market quickly reprices expectations.
• If the outcome is better than feared, stocks often rally sharply as uncertainty disappears.
• If the data surprises negatively, markets can dip further as investors adjust to higher inflation or weaker growth.

In simple terms:

• Fear often builds before the event,
• Volatility spikes at the release,
• Markets frequently rally once uncertainty clears.
    
You can find them under the Market Calendar yield in the Short-Term Signals tab for quick reference and trading opportunities.

lessons.id: How to Research Market Direction and Hedge Events?
lessons.title: How to Research Market Direction and Hedge Events?
lessons.body:
How to research the next market move

Reviewed October 14, 2026

Forecast the surprise, not just the headline
Start with the calendar, consensus expectations, the range of forecasts and the market’s recent reaction to similar news. Compare the actual release with what investors expected, not only with the previous reading. A strong economy can support earnings while keeping interest rates high; weak data can ease rate expectations while raising recession concerns. The same headline can therefore produce different market reactions in different regimes.

Map inflation, jobs and the Fed
For CPI and PPI, distinguish monthly changes from annual changes and headline from underlying components. For employment, review payrolls, wages, unemployment and revisions together. BLS seasonal adjustments can revise historical CPI readings, so save the data vintage used in research. For the Fed, separate the rate decision from guidance, projections and the press conference. The Federal Reserve explains that expected policy, not just today’s rate, affects longer-term rates and asset prices.

Build three scenarios before the date
Write a constructive, mixed and adverse scenario, with the evidence that would support each one. For example, softer inflation alongside resilient activity might support equities; softer inflation with worsening employment might instead raise growth concerns. Describe the expected response in Treasury yields, the dollar, market breadth and relevant sectors. These are hypotheses to check after the release, not mechanical trading rules. Distinguish the first minutes of reaction from the closing move and the following sessions.

Check the market environment
Compare the S&P 500 with QQQ, sector participation, breadth, credit conditions and volatility. Concentrated leadership may make an index vulnerable even when its headline price looks strong. Use options-implied moves as a rough indication of priced uncertainty, not a directional forecast. Historical event studies should separate inflation and growth regimes, include losing observations, account for costs and avoid using revised data that was unavailable at the time.

Position ahead of the event—with a risk budget
Before the calendar date, review concentration, correlated positions, liquidity and the loss your portfolio could sustain in an adverse scenario. Decide whether to reduce exposure, keep cash, hold through the event or hedge. Define the hedge horizon, cost budget and conditions for removing it before placing an order. Pre-event selling and post-event rallies are possible, not a dependable sequence. Stops can fill below their trigger during gaps; being early does not guarantee a better outcome.

Choose the hedge that fits the exposure
A protective put on shares you own can limit downside below its strike through expiry, at the cost of a premium. A collar adds a covered call to help fund the put, but caps upside and introduces assignment risk. A broad-index hedge may only partly offset a concentrated portfolio; correlations and option sensitivity change. Compare expiry, strike, premium, spreads and position size. Puts can lose value through time decay or falling implied volatility even when stocks decline modestly. Volatility-linked products are not direct ownership of spot VIX and require separate research into their structure.

Update the forecast after the release
Compare the actual data and revisions with your scenarios. Check whether bond yields, breadth and price action support the first move. Reduce confidence when signals conflict, and reassess if the expected mechanism does not appear. Keep a dated journal of the forecast, evidence, hedge cost and outcome. A useful process measures calibration and drawdowns as well as directional accuracy; it does not promise to predict every session.

Official sources
Federal Reserve: how monetary policy works
https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/monetary-policy-what-are-its-goals-how-does-it-work.htm

BLS: CPI seasonal adjustments
https://www.bls.gov/cpi/seasonal-adjustment/

lessons.title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
lessons.description: Measures inflation at the consumer level.
lessons.body:
The CPI (Consumer Price Index) report measures the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a basket of goods and services.
      
It is a key economic indicator used to track inflation and the cost of living, and is typically released ahead of the FED meeting (FOMC explained in the onboarding).
      
The CPI includes various categories, such as:

	•	Food and Beverages: Groceries, meals away from home, etc.

	•	Housing: Rent, owners’ equivalent rent, utilities.

	•	Transportation: Gas, car insurance, public transportation.

	•	Medical Care: Health insurance, prescription drugs, etc.

	•	Recreation, Education, and Other: Entertainment, educational services, etc.

The CPI is released monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), with the Core CPI (which excludes food and energy prices) often used as a more accurate measure of underlying inflation trends.

How Does It Affect the Stock Market?

1.	Inflation Expectations:

  •	Rising CPI: Higher CPI indicates rising inflation, which may prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to cool the economy. Rising rates typically have a negative impact on stock prices, especially for growth stocks, which are sensitive to higher borrowing costs.

  •	Falling CPI: A lower-than-expected CPI indicates reduced inflationary pressures, which may be seen as positive for the economy. It could lead to expectations that the Fed will ease monetary policy, often resulting in a market rally.

2.	Interest Rates and Monetary Policy:
	
	•	High Inflation: Persistent high CPI readings suggest inflation is not under control, which could lead to more aggressive rate hikes by the Fed. This is negative for equities, particularly for sectors reliant on low interest rates.
	
	•	Moderate Inflation: A moderate CPI growth rate suggests inflation is under control and the Fed might not raise rates as aggressively. This is often positive for the market.
	
	•	Deflationary Pressures: If CPI shows signs of deflation (falling prices), it could signal weak demand in the economy, which could hurt corporate earnings and lead to a market decline.
	
3.	Sectoral Impact:

	•	Growth/Tech Stocks: Higher inflation (reflected in CPI) can negatively affect growth stocks, particularly tech companies, because rising interest rates reduce the present value of future earnings. 

	•	Consumer Staples: Companies in defensive sectors, like consumer staples, may see less of a negative impact from rising CPI because people will still need to purchase essential items, regardless of inflation.

	•	Financials: Banks and financial institutions can benefit from inflation if it leads to higher interest rates, which widen their profit margins on loans.

	•	Commodities: CPI may affect commodity prices, as inflation often leads to higher demand for commodities like gold or oil as a hedge against currency devaluation.

4.	Volatility:

	•	CPI reports often lead to significant market reactions. Unexpected CPI results (either higher or lower than forecast) can lead to increased volatility in stocks, bonds, and commodities.

How to Trade the CPI Report?

Often the stock market will dip ahead of reports due to uncertainties
	
1.	Before the Report:

	•	Monitor Expectations: Analysts and economists forecast CPI each month. If the market expects a high CPI and the actual reading is lower, the market could rally. Conversely, a higher-than-expected CPI can lead to a sell-off.

	•	Options and Futures: If you expect high volatility around the CPI release, consider options or futures strategies like straddles (buying both calls and puts) to profit from large moves in either direction.

2.	On Report Day:

	•	Focus on Core CPI: The market often reacts more to the Core CPI (which excludes volatile food and energy prices) because it gives a clearer picture of underlying inflation trends.

	•	Watch for Market Reaction: Pay attention to how the market reacts immediately after the release, especially in sectors like tech (sensitive to interest rates) and financials (potential beneficiaries of rate hikes).

3.	Post-Report Strategy:

	•	Monitor Interest Rate Expectations: Follow market reactions regarding interest rate expectations. If CPI shows inflation is rising, markets may anticipate rate hikes. Adjust your positions based on whether you’re bullish or bearish on equities.

	•	Look for Sector Rotation: A higher-than-expected CPI may prompt a rotation into defensive sectors like consumer staples or utilities. Conversely, a lower-than-expected CPI could shift funds into growth or cyclical stocks.

	•	Use ETFs: Consider trading ETFs like SPY (S&P 500), QQQ (NASDAQ), or IWM (Russell 2000) to capture market-wide movements, or sector-specific ETFs if you believe certain sectors will benefit more from the CPI results.

4.	Long-Term View:

	•	Trend Analysis: If CPI consistently rises month after month, inflationary pressures may continue to build, leading to a prolonged period of higher interest rates. Conversely, a consistent decline in CPI might signal deflationary trends or an economic slowdown, which could impact long-term growth expectations.

	•	Fed Policy: Understand that the Federal Reserve’s actions will likely be heavily influenced by CPI data. A prolonged high CPI could lead to more aggressive rate hikes, while a lower CPI could signal a pause in tightening, supporting a bullish market outlook.

Key Tips:

	•	Stay Informed: Keep track of the market’s expectations for CPI by looking at forecasts and the market’s implied inflation expectations.

	•	Use Volatility to Your Advantage: The market tends to react sharply to CPI surprises, so volatility can be used for profit with options or futures strategies.

	•	Look for Confirmation from Other Economic Data: CPI is just one piece of the economic puzzle. Always consider other indicators like GDP growth, unemployment data, and Fed statements before making large trades.

By understanding how CPI affects inflation expectations and the broader economy, traders can better position themselves for short-term moves or long-term trends.

lessons.title: Producer Price Index (PPI)
lessons.description: Tracks price changes for producers.
lessons.body:
The PPI (Producer Price Index) measures the average change over time in the selling prices received by domestic producers for their output.

It’s a key inflation indicator focused on **wholesale prices**, and is often seen as a leading indicator for future consumer inflation (CPI).

The PPI includes major industry categories like:

  • Manufacturing
  • Mining and Energy
  • Agriculture
  • Services (less emphasized)

Unlike the CPI, which measures prices from the consumer’s perspective, the PPI reflects price changes from the producer’s point of view — before they reach the end consumer.

PPI data is released monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), with Core PPI (excluding food and energy) often used for a clearer signal on inflation trends.


Why Does PPI Matter for the Stock Market?

1. Inflation Insight Ahead of CPI:

   • Rising PPI suggests cost pressures for companies, which can later be passed onto consumers (eventually affecting CPI).
   
   • Markets view higher PPI as a precursor to inflation, increasing expectations of **Fed rate hikes.

2. Profit Margins:

   • If PPI rises and companies can’t pass on costs to consumers, profit margins shrink — bad for stocks.
   
   • If PPI rises but revenue grows faster, it may signal healthy demand — neutral or even positive.

3. Interest Rate Sensitivity:

   • Just like CPI, rising PPI adds pressure on the Fed to keep interest rates higher for longer.
   
   • Sectors sensitive to borrowing costs (e.g., tech, real estate) often react negatively to hot PPI numbers.

4. Sector Impacts:

   • **Industrials & Materials**: Directly impacted by rising input costs.
   
   • **Consumer Staples**: Often able to pass on rising prices to customers.
   
   • **Tech & Growth Stocks**: Vulnerable to rising rate expectations from inflation data like PPI.



How to Trade the PPI Report

1. Before the Report:

   • Monitor analyst forecasts — a surprise in either direction can cause strong market moves.
   
   • Expect increased volatility, especially in inflation-sensitive sectors.

2. On Report Day:

   • Focus on Core PPI and **MoM trends** — markets react more to surprises in Core data.
   
   • Look for bond yield reactions — rising yields often weigh on equities.

3. Post-Report Strategy:

   • If PPI comes in hot, consider hedging (e.g., SPY puts or VIX calls).
   
   • Watch for sector rotation** — defensive sectors may outperform if inflation fears rise.

4. Long-Term View:

   • Consistently high PPI could lead to longer-lasting rate hikes, affecting corporate investment and valuations.
   
   • Consistent declines in PPI may signal a cooling economy or deflationary risks, affecting sentiment and earnings outlook.

---

Key Tips:

   • PPI is often a **precursor** to CPI — watch for signs that wholesale inflation is feeding into consumer prices.

   • Use tools like sector ETFs or options to position for volatility (e.g., XLI for industrials, SPY or QQQ for index exposure).

   • Pair PPI insights with other economic data for confirmation: CPI, jobs data, Fed minutes, and earnings trends.

By understanding the PPI report, traders can anticipate how inflation pressures may affect markets before CPI hits — giving them a valuable edge in timing and positioning.

lessons.title: Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)
lessons.description: Federal Reserve interest rate decisions.
lessons.body:
The FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) report summarizes the decisions made during the Federal Reserve’s policy-setting meetings.
      
These meetings typically occur eight times a year and include discussions about:
      
  •	Interest rate policy: Whether to raise, lower, or maintain the federal funds rate.
  
  •	Economic outlook: Projections on inflation, employment, GDP growth, and other key metrics.
  
  •	Monetary policy adjustments: Measures like quantitative easing or tightening.
  
  •	Summary of Economic Projections (SEP): Provided at select meetings, showing forecasts for inflation, unemployment, and interest rates.

The report, particularly the FOMC Statement and Minutes, provides valuable insights into the Fed’s perspective on the U.S. economy and their policy direction.

How Does It Affect the Stock Market?

1.	Interest Rate Changes:

  •	Rate Hikes: Raising interest rates makes borrowing more expensive, which can slow down economic growth. This often negatively affects stock prices over the short term, especially for growth and tech stocks reliant on cheap credit. However this usually happens in period of high inflation.and the effect is balance by the positive impact of inflation on stocks.

  •	Rate Cuts: Lowering rates reduces borrowing costs, stimulating spending and investment, which generally boosts stock prices and stimulates the economy when inflation slows down.

2.	Market Sentiment:

  •	The Fed’s tone (hawkish or dovish) heavily influences market sentiment. A hawkish tone (focused on controlling inflation) may signal tighter monetary policy, often causing stock sell-offs. A dovish tone (stimulating growth) can result in rallies.

3.	Sectoral Impact:

  •	Financial Sector: Banks benefit from rising rates as they can earn more from loans.

  •	Growth/Tech Stocks: Companies relying on future cash flows (e.g., tech) are hurt by higher rates, as their valuations (long term membership spread over 10 years+) are negatively impacted by higher discount rates.

  •	Defensive/Consumer Retail Stocks: Sectors like utilities or consumer staples may perform better in volatile periods triggered by FOMC decisions.

4.	Volatility:

  •	The market often experiences sharp swings on the day of the FOMC release as traders react to new information.

How to Trade the FOMC Report?

1.	Before the Announcement:

Often stocks will dip right before the announcement due to uncertainties:
  
  •	Monitor Expectations: Look at futures markets or tools like the CME FedWatch Tool, which gauges the probability of rate changes. If the market is expecting a hike but the Fed signals a pause, stocks may rally unexpectedly.
  
  •	Position Accordingly: Avoid speculative positions if you’re unsure, as FOMC days are notoriously volatile.

2.	On Announcement Day:

  •	Pay Attention to the Statement: Read the language carefully to determine whether the tone is hawkish or dovish. Key phrases like “higher for longer” for rates can trigger sell-offs.
  
  •	Watch the Press Conference: Comments from the Fed Chair (e.g., Jerome Powell) often provide deeper insight into the Fed’s thinking.

3.	Post-Announcement Reaction:

  •	Monitor Key Levels: Stock indices like the S&P 500 often establish a range post-FOMC. Look for breakouts or reversals.
  
  •	Focus on Sectors: Adjust your portfolio based on which sectors are likely to benefit or suffer from the Fed’s direction.

4.	Use Volatility Tools:

  •	Trade ETFs like the VIX for volatility exposure.
  
  •	Use options strategies, such as straddles or strangles (explained in the options onboarding), to capitalize on large market moves!

5.	Long-Term View:

  •	Incorporate FOMC projections into your macroeconomic analysis. For example, if the Fed signals prolonged rate hikes, consider defensive assets like bonds or dividend-paying stocks.

Key Tips:

•	Avoid Overtrading: The FOMC report often triggers exaggerated moves; stick to your strategy.

•	Hedge Your Bets: Use stop-losses or diversify positions to protect against unexpected outcomes.

•	Be Patient: Often, the best trading opportunities arise not during the announcement, but after the initial market reaction settles.

By understanding the Fed’s intentions and their implications on the economy, traders can better navigate market movements and align their strategies with prevailing trends.

lessons.title: Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP)
lessons.description: Monthly employment report impacting markets.
lessons.body:
The Employment Situation Report is a monthly Macro Economic report released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
      
It provides critical insights into the U.S. labor market, including key data points like:

Key Components:

	1.	Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP): Measures the change in the number of jobs in the U.S. economy, excluding farm workers, government employees, private households, and nonprofit organizations.
	
	2.	Unemployment Rate: The percentage of the labor force that is unemployed but actively seeking work.
	
	3.	Average Hourly Earnings: Tracks wage growth, which can signal inflationary pressures.
	
	4.	Labor Force Participation Rate: Indicates the percentage of the working-age population that is working or actively looking for work.

Impact on Stock Markets:

	1.	Positive Surprise (Stronger Labor Data):
	
	•	Indicates a robust economy.
	•	Can lead to higher stock prices in cyclical sectors (like financials and industrials) if the data shows strong job growth without overheating inflation.
	•	However, strong data may lead to concerns about the Federal Reserve increasing interest rates, which could negatively affect growth stocks.
	
	2.	Negative Surprise (Weaker Labor Data):
	
	•	Suggests a slowing economy, often leading to a sell-off in equities, particularly in cyclical stocks.
	•	Defensive sectors like utilities and consumer staples may outperform.
	•	Weak data may fuel expectations of monetary easing, boosting tech stocks and other rate-sensitive assets.
	
	3.	Wage Inflation (Higher Average Hourly Earnings):
	•	Suggests potential inflationary pressures.
	•	Often leads to fears of tighter monetary policy, negatively impacting stocks.

How to Trade the NFP Report:

	1.	Pre-NFP Setup:
	
	•	Most of the times the stock market will dip ahead of the report due to uncertainties. Analyze market expectations by reviewing consensus forecasts from analysts.
	
	•	Monitor related indicators like ADP Employment Change and weekly jobless claims for a sense of the labor market.
	
	2.	During the Release:
	
	•	Expect heightened volatility across major indices, currencies (especially USD), and commodities (like gold and oil).
	
	•	Focus on deviations from the expected figures. A surprise in any key component (like NFP, unemployment rate, or wages) can cause sharp moves.
	
	3.	Trading Strategies:
	
	•	Scalping Volatility: Use tight stop-losses to capitalize on rapid price movements right after the report is released.
	
	•	Breakout Trading: Place pending buy and sell orders around key support/resistance levels, expecting a breakout due to high volatility.
	
	•	Trend-Following Post-Release: Once the market digests the data, follow the established trend.
	
	4.	Hedging:
	
	•	Options can be used to hedge against unexpected volatility.
	
	For example, buying both call and put options (a straddle - explained in the Options Onboarding) before the release can profit from large moves in either direction.

Key Markets to Watch:

	•	Stock Market Indices: S&P 500, Dow Jones, Nasdaq.
	
	•	Forex: USD currency pairs (like EUR/USD, USD/JPY).
	
	•	Commodities: Gold often reacts to NFP due to its relationship with interest rates and the dollar.
	
	•	Bonds: U.S. Treasury yields, especially the 2-year and 10-year, as they reflect expectations of Fed policy.

Tips for Success:

	1.	Understand Context: Know whether the Fed is hawkish or dovish. This will affect how the market interprets strong or weak data.
	
	2.	Avoid Over-Leveraging: Volatility can lead to sharp, unpredictable moves.
	
	3.	Focus on Quality Data: Watch revisions to previous reports, as they can also move markets.

By incorporating NFP insights from our app into your trading strategy, you can position yourself to take advantage of the market’s reaction to one of the most impactful economic indicators.

lessons.id: Why Does Inclusion in the S&P 500 Matter?
lessons.title: Why Does Inclusion in the S&P 500 Matter?
lessons.description: Index inclusion can trigger institutional buying.
lessons.body:
Inclusion in the S&P 500 is significant because of the ripple effects it creates in the financial markets:

1.	Increased Demand for Shares:
•	Funds and ETFs that track the S&P 500 must purchase shares of the newly included stock, leading to a price surge from increased demand.
•	This “index effect” often drives the stock price higher shortly after the announcement.

2.	Greater Visibility:
•	Inclusion signals that a company is among the largest, most stable, and reputable in the U.S. economy.
•	This increases investor confidence and may attract more long-term institutional investors.

3.	Liquidity Boost:
•	Higher trading volumes make it easier for investors to buy and sell shares.

4.	Market Impact:
•	The inclusion reflects positively on the company’s fundamentals (e.g., profitability, stability) and acts as a stamp of approval from the market.

lessons.id: How to Profit from S&P 500 Inclusions?
lessons.title: How to Profit from S&P 500 Inclusions?
lessons.description: Strategies around index rebalancing events.
lessons.body:
How to Profit from S&P 500 Inclusions

1.	Anticipating the Announcement:
•	Research candidates: Analyze companies that meet S&P 500 criteria and are likely candidates for inclusion.
•	Potential candidates may already show strong fundamentals, steady growth, and sector relevance.
•	Buy shares before an official announcement to benefit from the price jump.

2.	After the Announcement:
•	Stocks included in the index often see a price surge following the announcement.
•	Traders can enter immediately after the news and sell shortly before or after the effective inclusion date to capitalize on the momentum.
•	Monitor technical indicators, as prices may dip once the initial buying frenzy cools off.

3.	Options Trading:
•	Use call options if you anticipate a price increase but want to limit your capital exposure.
•	After the inclusion is announced, implied volatility tends to rise, presenting opportunities for options strategies.

4.	Short-Term vs. Long-Term Gains:
•	Short-term: Focus on the immediate price movement following the announcement.
•	Long-term: Some stocks benefit from sustained interest due to higher liquidity and inclusion in passive investment portfolios.

5.	Be Cautious of the “Post-Inclusion Dip”:
•	After the stock is added to the index and demand from funds is met, prices often decline (“post-inclusion effect”).
•	Traders who hold too long risk losses when the buying frenzy subsides.

6.	Avoid the Hype:
•	Not all stocks skyrocket after inclusion; some may already have inclusion “priced in” due to speculation.

lessons.title: How to Predict Index Inclusions?
lessons.description: Research Russell, S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 candidates before announcements.
lessons.body:
How to predict which stocks could join an index

Reviewed October 14, 2026

**Start with a shortlist, not a certainty**
Index research starts with eligibility, then ranking, then the announcement calendar. A candidate is not a confirmed addition, and inclusion does not guarantee a price rise. This guide covers Russell U.S. indexes, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100—the index tracked by QQQ, not the entire Nasdaq Composite.

**Russell**

Rebuild the eligible universe
Screen for eligible U.S. companies, exchanges and security types, then apply the current investability rules. Rank eligible companies by total market capitalization at the official rank date; use float-adjusted capitalization for weights. The Russell 1000 broadly represents the largest 1,000 companies and the Russell 2000 the next 2,000. Apply the provider’s banding and migration rules instead of assuming every company crossing rank 1,000 changes indexes. Starting in 2026, reconstitution occurs in June and December; IPO additions also have a separate process. Build a watchlist around the relevant boundaries, stress-test price and share-count changes, and compare it with preliminary lists before treating additions as confirmed.

**S&P 500**

Eligibility comes before committee selection
Check U.S. domicile, eligible listing and share type, current market-cap and float requirements, liquidity and IPO seasoning. For ordinary corporate candidates, GAAP income from continuing operations must be positive in the latest quarter and across the latest four quarters combined; REIT provisions differ. Use the provider’s current thresholds rather than an old fixed market-cap cutoff. Eligibility does not secure a seat: the index committee also considers representation of the market. Watch potential vacancies, mergers and sector balance, but do not present a ranking as the committee’s decision. Changes can happen during the year. Separate an eligible shortlist from an official addition announcement.

**Nasdaq-100**

Rank candidates and account for incumbents
Start with eligible Nasdaq-listed, non-financial companies. Check security type, liquidity, listing seasoning and other eligibility rules before ranking by full company market capitalization at the reference date. At the annual December reconstitution, the top 75 are selected first. Existing members in the top 100 are retained; qualifying incumbents ranked 101–125 can also retain a place under the methodology’s prior-ranking conditions. Remaining places are filled from eligible non-members in the top 100. This is why being the 100th-largest candidate is not enough. Quarterly weight rebalances are different from annual membership selection, and replacements can occur between reviews.

**Build a repeatable research process**
Record the methodology version, data timestamp and upcoming rank, announcement and effective dates. Reconcile share counts, corporate actions, float and industry classification against filings. Run a base case and alternative price/share-count scenarios; document why each candidate passes or fails. Use news and Wall Street research to investigate mergers, exchange transfers and changing eligibility—not to override official rules. Label the result “candidate,” “preliminary” or “confirmed,” with the evidence and date beside it. Validate the approach on past reviews using only data available at the time, tracking false positives as well as successful calls. Do not publish a numerical probability unless the model has been calibrated out of sample.

**Estimate demand separately from membership**
As a research scenario, approximate tracking demand using assets actually tracking the index multiplied by the proposed change in weight, then divide by share price. Adjust for positions already held, fund overlap, sampling and implementation differences. Compare estimated shares with normal trading volume and available float. This is an approximation of potential flows, not a price target. Anticipation, arbitrage, wider market moves and selling after implementation can overwhelm the effect. A correct membership prediction can still produce a losing trade.

**Official sources**
FTSE Russell: reconstitution calendar and methodology
https://www.lseg.com/en/ftse-russell/russell-reconstitution

S&P U.S. Indices Methodology
https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/methodologies/methodology-sp-us-indices.pdf

Nasdaq-100 methodology
https://indexes.nasdaq.com/docs/Methodology_NDX.pdf

lessons.title: Stock Buy Backs
lessons.description: Companies repurchasing shares to increase value.
lessons.body:
Stock buy backs happen when a company repurchases its stock from shareholders!

It shows the company values its share price and have enough cash to buy them back.

This pushes the value of the share price up because there will be less shares on the market (because the value of the company = shares available x price of each share, remains the same)!

Since the company will be repurchasing their shares (after you) a trading opportunity happens right after the announcement (AI will send you buy signals)!

Apple stock price rallied +15% after latest stock buy back announcement!

lessons.title: Stock Split
lessons.body:
Buy Nvidia before the 1-10 split!🧠

The same patterns happened with each stock split, Nvidia, Tesla and others:

👉 A 1-10 stock split is a corporate action in which a company turns 1 share of each stock into 10,

👉 Share price will be 10 times lower (because the company valuation = share price x numbers of shares, remains the same).

However human psychology could affect the company prospects and make the share price rally towards its growth in earnings per share, which is why companies do it when they had hue growth (just like Nvidia and Tesla did).

Unit bias is a psychological phenomenon where investors perceive the value of an investment based on the price of its shares rather than its overall market capitalization.

Often people are looking for shares 'under $100' which helps push the price up after the stock split (buy as soon as it's announced)!

lessons.title: Dividend Announcements
lessons.description: Corporate dividend payments to shareholders.
lessons.body:
Dividends are a portion of a company’s earnings distributed to shareholders as a reward for their investment!

A company announces dividends when it has strong financial health and positive cash flow, signaling confidence in its future prospects.

Receiving dividends provides shareholders with a steady income stream in addition to any capital gains from rising stock prices.

Dividend announcements often lead to a rise in share price, as they indicate financial stability and profitability, making the stock more attractive to investors.

Historically, companies like Johnson & Johnson and Coca-Cola, and more recently Google and Meta, have seen their stock prices increase following dividend announcements due to the market’s positive reception!

lessons.title: Mergers and Acquisitions
lessons.description: Corporate deals impacting stock prices.
lessons.body:
When one company acquires another, the stock price of the acquiring company tends to dip temporarily, while the stock price of the target company tends to spike.

The acquiring company's share price drops because it often pays a premium for the target company, or incurs debt to finance the acquisition.

The target company's short-term share price tends to rise because the shareholders only agree to the deal if the purchase price exceeds their company's current value.

M&A setups often trigger “buy the rumor, sell the news” behavior.

Prices keep moving on speculation when deals are rumored but not confirmTap ed, then reprice quickly once final terms are announced.

The edge comes from positioning early and managing exits as the catalyst plays out.

Over the long haul, an acquisition tends to boost the acquiring company's share price.

lessons.title: Private Placement
lessons.description: Capital raising through private investors.
lessons.body:
A private placement is when a company raises money by selling shares directly to select investors (like institutions or high-net-worth individuals), instead of through a public offering.

Short-Term Effect:

•	Stocks often dip temporarily after the announcement.
•	Why? Because new shares are usually issued at a discount, causing short-term dilution.

Long-Term Potential:

•	If used wisely, the raised capital helps fund growth projects, R&D, or acquisitions.
•	This can lead to strong long-term rallies, especially if the company executes well.

Common in Small Caps:

•	When small-cap stocks rally quickly, companies often use the momentum to raise funds at favorable valuations.
•	This strategy helps them scale faster without taking on debt.

lessons.title: Convertible Notes Issuance
lessons.description: Capital raised through convertible debt.
lessons.body:
A convertible notes issuance is when a company raises money by selling debt (notes) that can later be converted into shares at a predefined price.

Short-Term Effect:

• Stocks often dip temporarily after the announcement.
• Why? Investors may fear future dilution if the notes convert into shares, and financing can create short-term uncertainty.

Long-Term Potential:

• If deployed well, the capital can fund expansion, AI infrastructure, acquisitions, or growth initiatives.
• This can drive strong long-term upside if revenue and profitability accelerate.

Less Dilutive Than Equity Raises:

• Unlike a traditional share offering, convertible notes start as debt and only convert into equity under certain conditions.
• Companies often use them when they expect strong future growth and want to raise large amounts at attractive terms.

Common in High-Growth Companies:

• Fast-growing tech and AI companies often use convertible notes to scale quickly while minimizing immediate shareholder dilution.
• Strong momentum stocks sometimes use rallies to secure capital for aggressive expansion.

lessons.title: What are 13F filings?
lessons.description: Compare quarterly institutional holdings and distinguish disclosed changes from possible future purchases.
lessons.body:
13F filings disclose eligible institutional holdings at quarter-end, generally filed within 45 days. They are delayed snapshots, not live portfolios.

Compare share counts across consecutive quarters, adjusted for splits. A higher dollar value alone may reflect a price rise, not buying. Repeated share increases can suggest accumulation, but cannot prove regular DCA or predict the next purchase.

For Berkshire and Alphabet, or Nvidia’s disclosed investments, first verify the filer, quarter and actual holdings. Do not assume Buffett personally selected every Berkshire position.

Use #13f feed posts alongside the app calendar. Watch the next disclosure, valuation and downside; expected buying remains a scenario until confirmed. Filings do not show a complete portfolio, exact trade dates or short equity positions.

lessons.title: What are 14f filings?
lessons.description: Disclosures about changes in a company’s board majority.
lessons.body:
A 14f-1 filing is a type of information statement that a company must file with the SEC when there is a change in the majority of its board of directors due to an acquisition or takeover.

Key Points:

• Purpose: It’s used to notify shareholders about the upcoming change in control of the board, providing transparency during a potential takeover or merger.

• Content: The filing includes information about the new directors, their backgrounds, and any agreements or plans between the acquiring company and the target company.

• Timing: It must be filed at least 10 days before the new directors officially take their positions.

This filing ensures that investors are informed about significant changes in the company’s governance, especially when a hedge fund or another entity is involved in acquiring control.

lessons.id: How to steal stock ideas from hedge funds
lessons.title: How to steal stock ideas from hedge funds
lessons.description: Use hedge fund portfolios as idea sources.
lessons.body:
Hedge funds can be a useful source of ideas, especially when several high-quality funds build positions in the same stock.

Here is how to use hedge fund data wisely:

1) Look for conviction: focus on stocks that represent meaningful portfolio weights, not tiny tracking positions.

2) Compare multiple funds: if several strong investors own the same name, that often matters more than one isolated position.

3) Check the business quality: strong EPS growth, improving revenues, and reasonable valuation still matter.

4) Be careful with delays: public filings are backward-looking, so use them as idea generation, not instant buy signals.

5) Use the app tools: compare holdings, valuation, momentum, and predictions before taking action.

The best use of hedge fund portfolios is not blind copying — it is finding high-conviction ideas, then validating them with your own analysis.

lessons.id: How to Research Potential Hedge Fund Buys?
lessons.title: How to Research Potential Hedge Fund Buys?
lessons.description: Build a 13F watchlist from disclosed share changes and verify future additions.
lessons.body:
What could hedge funds buy next?

Reviewed October 14, 2026

**The next filing starts with the last one**

Build a manager-specific watchlist rather than a generic list of famous holdings. Compare several quarters of split-adjusted share counts, new positions, exits and portfolio weights. Separate an increase in shares from a rise in the stock price. Repeated additions can suggest accumulation, but do not prove dollar-cost averaging or a commitment to buy again. This is a research framework, not access to a fund’s orders.

**Combine position history with public catalysts**

Look for shareholder letters, public interviews, company announcements, earnings revisions, product launches and industry developments that fit the manager’s disclosed investment approach. Check whether an existing position is small enough to expand relative to that manager’s historical concentration, and whether liquidity permits it. A public activist campaign can strengthen a thesis; an acquisition, mandate change or redemptions can weaken it. Date every piece of evidence and distinguish the manager’s own statements from speculation.

**A more disciplined candidate score**

Use an evidence checklist: persistence of share-count increases, relevance to the manager’s mandate, valuation change since the last disclosure, company catalysts, liquidity and counter-evidence. Keep accumulation candidates separate from entirely new-name candidates. Do not turn this checklist into a percentage probability without historical calibration. Test it using only information available before each filing; compare false positives and missed positions against a simple baseline such as unchanged holdings.

**Prepare your positioning plan before the filing date**

Mark the expected filing window and prepare your watchlist, valuation range, maximum exposure and invalidation conditions ahead of it. If considering a position before disclosure, size it for the possibility that the fund did not buy—or already sold. Staged entries can reduce dependence on one entry price, but averaging down increases exposure and does not repair a broken thesis. Waiting for confirmation is a valid choice. The goal is to have a plan before the date, not to buy automatically because a deadline is approaching.

**What a 13F can—and cannot—tell you**

Form 13F is generally due within 45 days of quarter-end. It describes reportable holdings at quarter-end, not holdings on filing day. Short equity positions and written options are not reported; confidential treatment and amendments can also affect the picture. A reported long holding is not the manager’s complete net exposure. The filing does not reveal exact execution prices or every trade during the quarter. Check the reporting period, security type and amendments before comparing positions.

**After release: compare evidence with your hypothesis**

Match the new filing to your shortlist. Reconcile share classes, splits, options versus common shares and reporting-manager changes before interpreting a position change. Record confirmed additions, unchanged holdings and reductions. Revisit your own valuation and risk budget even when the prediction was correct: publicity may already be reflected in the price, and the manager’s horizon or hedge may differ from yours.

**Official sources**

SEC: Form 13F FAQ
https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/frequently-asked-questions-about-form-13f
