lessons.id: Index Inclusion Playbook: How to Build and Test a Candidate List
lessons.title: Index Inclusion Playbook: How to Build and Test a Candidate List
lessons.description: Six index-specific checklists, worked scenarios and official methodology links.
lessons.body:
Turn eligibility rules into a dated, testable watchlist.

**Start in the app**
Open the Market calendar for indexation events and the “Who could join the index next?” learning section. The introductory lesson “How to Predict Index Inclusions?” covers the foundations. This Advanced & Edge playbook takes you through six major U.S. equity benchmarks with widely traded tracking products—not a ranking of their trading volume.

**Build your research sheet first**
For every candidate record: ticker, current membership, eligible listing, security type, shares outstanding, float, market capitalization, liquidity, earnings eligibility, reference date, announcement date and effective date. Save the methodology version and the source timestamp. Use only information available at your prediction date; never backfill a successful prediction with later data. All examples below are hypothetical research exercises.

1. S&P 500 — screen first, then assess selection
Check the current large-cap entry threshold, U.S. eligibility, float, liquidity and listing history. Apply the profitability test: positive latest-quarter GAAP earnings and positive combined last-four-quarter earnings, subject to methodology exceptions. Selection remains discretionary.
Example: XYZ has just reported a profitable quarter. Recompute its trailing four-quarter total, verify every other eligibility test, then examine vacancies and sector representation. Add it as eligible, not confirmed.
[Official S&P U.S. methodology](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/methodologies/methodology-sp-us-indices.pdf)

2. Nasdaq-100 — rank eligible companies, then apply retention rules
Start with eligible Nasdaq-listed non-financial companies. Verify listing seasoning, liquidity and security eligibility. Rank companies using the provider’s full-market-cap definition, including its share-class and ADR treatment. Apply current incumbent-retention and replacement rules rather than selecting the largest 100 mechanically. Check the current annual review and any applicable fast-entry provisions separately from weight rebalances.
Example: XYZ ranks 92nd on your reference-date sheet. That alone does not guarantee entry. Rebuild the selection with eligible incumbents, record remaining slots, then rerun with prices 10% higher and lower. If XYZ drops out in modest scenarios, label the candidacy fragile.
[Official Nasdaq-100 methodology](https://indexes.nasdaq.com/docs/Methodology_NDX.pdf)

3. Dow Jones Industrial Average — study representation and share price
The Dow holds 30 blue-chip companies and is price-weighted. A market-cap ranking is not a membership forecast. Review the committee’s criteria, sector representation, sustained business performance and the share price’s effect on index weight.
Example: a hypothetical stock split reduces XYZ from $900 to $150 per share. Recalculate the approximate weight against the sum of constituent prices in your proposed basket, then compare sector representation before and after a replacement. A more practical weight supports a scenario, not a scheduled addition. There is no predictable annual admission queue.
[Official Dow methodology](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/methodologies/methodology-dj-averages.pdf)

4. Russell 2000 — model the size boundaries
Build the eligible U.S. universe and rank by total market capitalization on the official rank date. The Russell 2000 broadly covers the next 2,000 companies after the Russell 1000. Apply investability, banding and migration rules; use float-adjusted capitalization for weights, not as a substitute for the membership ranking. From 2026, reviews are semiannual; check the official calendar for exact dates.
Example: XYZ moves from an estimated rank of 3,040 to 2,950. Reconcile its share count and eligibility, test nearby competitors and price changes, then compare your candidate list with preliminary announcements. Treat movement near rank 1,000 separately: migration can create buying by one set of funds and selling by another.
[Official Russell rules and resources](https://www.lseg.com/en/ftse-russell/indices/russell-us)
[Official Russell review calendar](https://www.lseg.com/en/ftse-russell/russell-reconstitution)

5. S&P MidCap 400 — track mid-cap eligibility and migrations
Apply the current mid-cap entry range and relevant S&P eligibility tests. Study potential vacancies and movements among S&P size segments.
Example: XYZ has grown beyond the small-cap entry range. Recheck eligibility and representation; growth alone does not force promotion. Separate a possible 400 addition from any 600 deletion when estimating flows.
[Official S&P MidCap 400 rules](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/methodologies/methodology-sp-us-indices.pdf)

6. S&P SmallCap 600 — do not copy a Russell shortlist
Apply the current small-cap range plus float, liquidity and financial-viability rules.
Example: XYZ meets a size screen but fails the earnings test. Keep it off your eligible shortlist until qualifying results are public. Russell membership alone does not establish S&P eligibility.
[Official S&P SmallCap 600 rules](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/methodologies/methodology-sp-us-indices.pdf)

**Estimate flows separately from predicting membership**
Illustrative calculation: $10 billion tracking an index × a hypothetical 0.10% new weight = $10 million of gross target exposure. At $50 per share, that is 200,000 shares; against 500,000 shares of normal daily volume, it equals 0.4 trading days. This is a scenario, not a measured order. Adjust for existing holdings, overlapping products, sampling, migrations and implementation timing; do not count the same assets twice. A weight is float-cap based for S&P/Russell, modified-cap based for Nasdaq-100 and price based for the Dow.

**Validate before calling it an edge**
Label each name candidate, preliminary or confirmed. Track false positives and missed additions across earlier reviews without using future data. Separate announcement-day and effective-date returns, subtract trading costs, and compare with an appropriate benchmark. Correctly predicting inclusion does not guarantee a profitable trade; anticipation and selling after implementation can overwhelm index demand.

lessons.id: How to Predict What a Hedge Fund Might Buy Before Disclosure?
lessons.title: How to Predict What a Hedge Fund Might Buy Before Disclosure?
lessons.description: Research possible accumulation before a filing, using portfolio history and public evidence.
lessons.body:
Build a watchlist before the filing arrives.

1. Start with the last portfolio
In Metrics → Smart Money → Tracker, open a manager and compare available quarters. Look for new positions, repeated additions, trims and exits. Compare share counts as well as weights: a rising stock price can increase a position’s value without any new buying. Berkshire’s portfolio is institutional, not Warren Buffett’s personal account.

2. Reassess the investment thesis
Review earnings, guidance, margins, cash flow, debt and valuation. Does the business still fit the manager’s investment objectives? Improving results and a reasonable price can support an accumulation hypothesis; weakening fundamentals or excessive concentration can support a reduction hypothesis. Recent stock performance alone is not enough.

3. Estimate the disclosure window
Review the manager’s historical filing dates alongside the official deadline. 13Fs are generally due within 45 days of quarter-end. Treat the historical pattern as an estimated window, not a promised date. The report describes quarter-end holdings, not today’s portfolio or exact trade dates.

4. Use unusual options activity as a clue
Compare contract volume with its normal activity and prior open interest; check strike, expiry, premium and subsequent open-interest changes. Repeated activity around a relevant catalyst can earn a place on your watchlist. It cannot identify the buyer as Berkshire or another fund. Calls may be sold, hedged or part of a spread, and activity near a filing may be unrelated to it. Verify current options data before drawing conclusions.

5. Build a scenario, then verify it
Hypothetical example: Berkshire began a position in XYZ. If later earnings strengthen its thesis, another addition is plausible. Repeated additions could resemble staged accumulation, but do not prove a DCA plan. Confirmation could attract attention; a price jump is not guaranteed and may already be priced in. Compare the next filing with your hypothesis and record what you got wrong.

In the app, also review the Market calendar for indexation signals and other catalysts. Index-related demand is a separate explanation from a fund choosing to buy.

Research possibilities, not private orders. 13Fs omit short positions and other assets, and holdings may change before publication.

lessons.id: How to Read Insider and Politician Trades Ahead of Earnings?
lessons.title: How to Read Insider and Politician Trades Ahead of Earnings?
lessons.description: Put disclosed trades in context around earnings and macro catalysts.
lessons.body:
Put the transaction on a timeline before treating it as a signal.

1. Open the stock’s activity
In Metrics, select a stock. Beside Financials and Technicals, open Insiders to review available insider, fund and politician disclosures. Compare them with the Earnings calendar and Market calendar for earnings and other macro catalysts.

2. Separate trade date from filing date
An insider purchase before earnings may only become public later. Most Form 4 transactions are reported within two business days. Congressional reports can arrive much later: generally within 30 days of notification and no later than 45 days after the trade. A disclosure published after earnings was not a signal available beforehand.

3. Read what actually happened
For insiders, distinguish open-market purchases from grants, option exercises and tax-related sales. Check the person’s role, position size, remaining ownership and any disclosed trading plan. Several independent buyers can be more informative than several rows from one transaction. Sales can reflect diversification or personal needs, not necessarily a negative company outlook.

4. Read politician disclosures carefully
Check whether the owner is the official, spouse or dependent, and whether the report describes stock or options. Amounts are often ranges, not exact investments. Committee membership or proximity to an event does not prove advance knowledge or explain the trade.

5. Connect activity with public evidence
Compare earnings expectations, guidance, valuation and price action. Ask what would support or contradict the idea. A purchase ahead of an event can coexist with disappointing results; an old disclosure may describe a position already changed.

Use the original filing and the app’s available records to build context. Missing records do not prove there was no activity, and reported trades are not guaranteed forecasts.

lessons.id: How to Find the Strongest Insider Signal Now?
lessons.title: How to Find the Strongest Insider Signal Now?
lessons.description: Use Smart Money Signals to shortlist meaningful, timely insider activity.
lessons.body:
Find the most interesting evidence to investigate—not simply the biggest headline.

1. Open the shortlist
Go to Metrics → Smart Money → Signals. Review the signal label, explanation, reporting dates and supporting records. Open the explanation to see why the signal was surfaced; the list is a research shortlist, not a live buy instruction or a calibrated probability of profit.

2. Prioritize meaningful buying
Look for genuine open-market purchases, several independent insiders buying, repeat purchases, and a meaningful increase relative to the buyer’s previous holdings. A CEO or CFO purchase can deserve attention, but seniority alone does not make it predictive. Compare size with that person’s usual activity, not just a dollar headline.

3. Remove misleading noise
Exclude grants and exercises from your purchase thesis, inspect planned transactions, and avoid counting amendments or related filings twice. A large sale is not automatically bearish. Check whether the signal is actually an insider trade, a politician disclosure or a quarterly fund-position change; these are different types of evidence.

4. Add the company context
Open the stock’s Financials and Technicals, then review earnings, cash flow, valuation, trend and liquidity. Use the Earnings and Market calendars to identify the next catalyst. A stronger research candidate combines credible buying evidence, a sound thesis and a price that still makes sense.

5. Check freshness before acting
Compare trade date, filing date, the app’s update time and the price move since the transaction. The most recently filed record may describe an older trade. Follow available tracker profiles for future filing alerts and reassess when new evidence arrives.

Write down why a candidate is interesting and what would invalidate it. “Hotter” means more compelling evidence to investigate—not a promise of better returns.

lessons.title: Bitcoin Calendar and Halving
lessons.description: Understand Bitcoin halving cycles and market impact.
lessons.body:
1) Major Bitcoin Surges:

- 2013 Surge:

In April 2013, Bitcoin's price surged from around $100 to over $1,000 within a few months, marking one of its first significant price rallies.

- 2020-2021 Bull Run:

Starting in late 2020 and continuing into early 2021, Bitcoin's price surged to new all-time highs, reaching around $60,000 in April 2021.

2) Major Bitcoin Crashes:

- December 2017 - February 2018:

After reaching an all-time high near $20,000 in December 2017, Bitcoin underwent a significant correction, dropping to around $6,000 by early February 2018.

- March 2020:

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, global markets experienced a sharp decline, and Bitcoin's price dropped from around $9,000 to nearly $4,000 within a couple of days in mid-March 2020.

- May 2021:

Following Elon Musk's announcement that Tesla would no longer accept Bitcoin as payment due to environmental concerns, Bitcoin's price plummeted from around $55,000 to below $30,000 within a few weeks.

3) Bitcoin Halving

Bitcoin halving is an event programmed into the Bitcoin protocol that occurs approximately every four years, or after every 210,000 blocks mined.

During a halving, the rewards that miners receive for validating transactions and adding blocks to the blockchain are halved.

The purpose of halving is to control the issuance rate of new Bitcoins, gradually reducing the rate at which new coins are created.

This mechanism ensures that the total supply of Bitcoin remains capped at 21 million coins, making it a deflationary asset.

The Bitcoin halving events have taken place as follows:

- November 28, 2012 (First Halving): The initial reward of 50 Bitcoins per block was reduced to 25 Bitcoins.

- July 9, 2016 (Second Halving): The block reward decreased from 25 Bitcoins to 12.5 Bitcoins.

- May 11, 2020 (Third Halving): The block reward was further reduced from 12.5 Bitcoins to 6.25 Bitcoins.

- The next Bitcoin halving is expected to occur approximately four years after the 2020 halving, in 2024.

- During this event, the block reward will be halved again, reducing the reward to 3.125 Bitcoins per block.

Halvings are significant events in the Bitcoin ecosystem as they impact the supply and potentially influence the asset's value.

The reduction in the rate of new Bitcoin creation often leads to discussions about its potential effects on the market dynamics and price.

This price prediction takes into account the effect of halving, but also social trend analysis explained below, and macro economics and current inflation rates.

lessons.title: Options Trading: Key Tips for Beginners
lessons.description: Essential option trading advice.
lessons.body:
Every stock research idea can also be traded using call options. When a stock price rises, call option prices generally rise as well. The difference is that options provide leverage, meaning they can amplify both gains (unlimited asynmetric upside) and losses (limited downside).

Where to find signals:

* "Signals" tab → "Stocks & Options Signals"
* Select "Options Predictions" to view suggested Strike and Maturity.  
* "Signals" tab → "Admin Insights"

How to choose the right option:

Your strike price and maturity should match your investment strategy:

1. Time Horizon

* Short-term view: ~1 month maturity
* Medium-term view: 3–6 months maturity
* Long-term view: 6–12 months (LEAPS)

Longer maturities provide more time for the investment thesis to play out and generally reduce time decay.

2. Position Size (amount invested)

* Higher strike prices: Higher potential returns, but higher short term risk (cf the "Options Predictions" convexity graph in the "Signals tab).
* Lower strike prices (near or in-the-money): Lower risk, higher probability of success, but lower convexity and upside.

Choose your Strike based on how much you’re comfortable risking.

3. Bid & Ask Spread

Always review the option chain before buying. Wide bid/ask spreads can significantly impact your entry price.

Review the Limit Orders, Market Orders, and Bid/Ask sections before placing your first options trade.

Beginner Guidelines

* Use small position sizes while gaining experience.
* Increase exposure gradually as your knowledge and confidence grow.

Remember: Options can generate larger returns than stocks, with tail signals delivering 30X to 100X overnight, but they also carry higher risk. Proper position sizing, patience, and disciplined execution are essential for long-term success.
